verseByVerse.commentary: The sevenfold confession is Trinitarian in structure: one Spirit (v. 4), one Lord/Christ (v. 5), one God and Father (v. 6). “One body” — the church is not a collection of individuals but a single organism. “One Spirit” — the same Spirit who sealed every believer indwells the whole without division. “One hope” — the eschatological destiny of all believers is identical; we run toward the same finish line. “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” — faith and baptism are not personal achievements but marks of belonging to the one Lord who claimed his people. The unity Paul urges in vv. 1–3 is not created by human effort; it is the visible expression of a unity grounded in the very life of the triune God.

verseByVerse.quote: one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.
verseByVerse.commentary: The sevenfold confession reaches its summit in the Father. Three prepositions describe three modes of his engagement with his world: over all (sovereignty, transcendence), through all (providential working in and through all things), in all (immanent presence). This is not pantheism but the living God who simultaneously transcends, sustains, and indwells his creation and his redeemed people. When the church fractures into factions, it contradicts the nature of the one God who is Father of all his children — which is why the plea for unity (vv. 1–3) is grounded here in the very character of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having called the church to unity, Paul introduces the glorious diversity that serves it — and its source is the most unexpected one imaginable: the triumphant, ascended, gift-giving Christ. Paul quotes Psalm 68, a victory psalm describing God ascending Mount Zion after defeating his enemies, distributing plunder to his people. He applies it to Christ: the One who descended to the lowest depths of the earth — to death itself, to the far country of human ruin — and then ascended far above all the heavens, has taken the spoils of his victory and distributed them as gifts to his beloved people. And the gifts are not impersonal endowments. They are people. Christ gives gifted persons to his church — apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers — as the ongoing fruit of his conquest.

But notice first what Paul calls the grace they carry: not saving grace — that has already been lavished in chapters 1–3 — but enabling grace, grace fitted for service, grace for ministry. And its source is Trinitarian: the gifts are given here by Christ the Son (vv. 7, 11); in 1 Corinthians 12 the same gifts flow from the Spirit (vv. 4, 11) and the Father (v. 6). One generosity, three Persons. The giftedness of every believer is a testimony to the Trinity.

And the ascended Christ who gives these gifts is himself the one who “fills all things” (v. 10) — plēroō ta panta. This is the great fullness theme that pulses through the whole letter: the church is his fullness (1:23), the goal of every believer is to be filled with all the fullness of God (3:19), the target of every ministry is the fullness of Christ (4:13). The mission of the exalted Lord is to fill all of creation with his presence, his glory, his life. The church is the first instalment of that filling. To serve in this body is to participate in the most significant project in the universe.

The four gifted offices — apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers — are not interchangeable. The apostles and prophets belong to the foundational era: they laid the once-for-all deposit of Scripture and revelation on which the whole church stands. The evangelists press outward to where the gospel has not yet reached. The pastor-teachers build up what remains, week by week, year by year, through patient feeding of the word. Each equips the saints in their own way: through the apostolic Scriptures, through the whole counsel of God applied to conscience and life, through training every member to be a witness, through the slow, faithful formation of souls.

And the purpose of this equipping subverts every instinct toward a passive, receiver-only congregation. The saints do the ministry; the gifted leaders equip the saints to do it. The congregation is not the audience; it is the army. The pastor is not the performer; he is the trainer. Diakonia — service — belongs to every member: serving the poor, encouraging the struggling, teaching and discipling one another, praying, giving, witnessing. No gift is too small. No calling too ordinary. The woman who visits the lonely widow, the man who opens his home for a small group, the teenager who shares the gospel with a classmate — all are building the body of Christ.

The goal is breathtaking: unity of the faith, full knowledge of the Son of God, mature manhood, nothing less than the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ (v. 13). Not a few exceptional souls reaching great heights, but the whole body — every member — growing together toward the complete image of Christ. This growth is mature, not merely numerical. It is deep, not merely wide. It means speaking the truth in love — not merely in a pleasant tone, but with the costly, goal-directed love that aims at the health of the other person and the glory of Christ, the love that risks the relationship for the sake of the soul (cf. Prov. 27:6; Gal. 4:16).

The result, when every part is working properly, is a body that builds itself up in love (v. 16): growing more mature, more loving, and more attractive to a watching world. Most of this growth is invisible — the unseen ligament, the quiet conversation, the faithful prayer. But it is real, and it is aimed at the most glorious end imaginable: a church that together reflects the full stature of Jesus Christ, the one who fills all things, until God is all in all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ascended Christ and the Equipping Ministry

The passage grounds all ministry in the ascension of Christ — a movement of Pauline theology that is often underemphasised. It is the ascended Christ who gives gifts to His church. The one who has "ascended far above all the heavens" (v.10) is also the one who "fills all things" — present everywhere, sovereign over all, distributing gifts according to His wisdom and His grace. Ministry is not primarily a human enterprise; it is a dimension of the ongoing, active reign of the risen and ascended King.

The list of gifted persons — apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers — has generated significant debate about which offices are permanent and which ceased with the apostolic age. The Reformed tradition has consistently held that the foundational offices (apostles and prophets, Ephesians 2:20) were unique to the founding of the church, while the equipping offices (evangelists, pastor-teachers) continue throughout the church's history. What remains constant in every age is the purpose: equipping the saints for ministry until the whole body reaches the fullness of Christ.

The metaphor of the body in vv.15–16 is Paul's most developed statement of mutual ministry. The body grows "when each part is working properly" — not when a few parts are exceptionally active while the rest remain passive, but when every member is fulfilling their function. This is the vision of a church in which every person is a minister — not because every person preaches, but because every person contributes the grace-gift they have received to the building up of the whole. The body that achieves this grows toward Christ in every way. The body that fails at this — where a few do everything and the many receive — stunts its own growth.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church had known extraordinary leadership — Paul himself had spent three years there, and the elders he had appointed knew the weight of shepherding a flock in a hostile city (Acts 20:28–31). Now Paul is gone, and his letter is itself an act of equipping: preparing the church to continue faithfully without his physical presence. The gifted leaders he describes in vv.11–12 are, in the first instance, the elders and teachers of the Ephesian church — men charged with the immense responsibility of preparing every member for a ministry that would build the body in Paul's absence. This was not a programme; it was a pastoral theology applied to a real community facing real challenges.

Now: The consumer church — where the congregation pays for spiritual services delivered by professional clergy — is the precise opposite of Paul's vision. It produces spiritual infants who cannot feed themselves, who are vulnerable to every wind of doctrine, who have no sense of their own giftedness or their own call to ministry. The equipping church — where gifted leaders deliberately, systematically invest in the ministry capacity of every member — produces a body that is robust, maturing, and growing in love. The question for every church leader is not "How well am I performing?" but "How well am I equipping?" And the question for every member is not "Am I being fed?" but "Am I contributing?"

verseByVerse.quote: But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The “but” is a pivot from the corporate unity of verses 1–6 to individual gifting. Diversity within unity. Hekastō — to each one, without exception. No member of the body is ungifted. The measure is determined by Christ; he gives as he sovereignly wills. This is not earned, not developed from natural talent alone, but graciously bestowed by the ascended Lord.

Notice carefully what Paul calls it: grace. But this is not saving grace — the grace of justification already lavished on the Ephesians in chapters 1–2. This is enabling grace: grace fitted for service, grace that equips each member to fulfil their particular calling in the body. The same word, but a distinct work. God’s grace does not stop at the threshold of salvation; it floods every room of the Christian life, including the room of ministry.

And mark the Trinitarian richness here. Paul says the gifts are given by Christ (v. 7, cf. v. 11 “he gave”). Yet in 1 Corinthians 12, the same gifts are distributed by the Spirit (vv. 4, 11) and their diversity traced to the Father (v. 6). Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — one divine generosity, flowing from three Persons. The giftedness of the church is itself a testimony to the Trinity. cf. 1 Cor. 12:4–6.

PREACHER’S NOTE The congregation may not feel gifted. This verse insists every believer has received grace for ministry. The question is not “do I have a gift?” but “am I using what Christ has given me?” And when they use it, they are drawing on the inexhaustible generosity of the triune God.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore it says, 'When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul quotes Psalm 68:18 — a psalm of divine-warrior triumph — and applies it to Christ’s ascension. The original psalm celebrated God’s victory over his enemies and triumphal procession to Zion. Paul sees this fulfilled and surpassed in Christ: the risen Lord has ascended “on high,” leading his defeated enemies in his train, and from the position of exaltation he now distributes gifts to his people. The cross was the decisive battle; the ascension is the triumphal procession; the gifts to the church are the spoils of war distributed to the victors. Ferguson: “The church’s gifts are not human resources organized for divine ends; they are the plunder of Christ’s victory given to his people.”

The textual adaptation preachers must address: The Hebrew of Psalm 68:18 reads läqa&htilde;tä mattanôt bä‘ädäm — “you received gifts from/among men.” The LXX follows the same sense. But Paul writes “he gave gifts to men.” This reversal is not a mistake; it is a deliberate and theologically informed adaptation. Three explanations converge: (1) The Targum tradition: the Aramaic Targum of Psalm 68:18 already rendered the verse “he gave gifts to the sons of men,” understanding Moses as the subject who received the Torah on Sinai and then distributed it to Israel. Paul, shaped by synagogue use of the psalm at Pentecost, follows this established interpretive tradition. (2) The logic of the conquering king: in the ancient world, when a victor returned in triumph, he received tribute from the defeated and then distributed gifts to his soldiers. “Receiving” and “giving” were two phases of the same event; the one who received the spoils immediately distributed them. Paul applies the distribution phase because that is the point of his argument: the ascended Christ gives to the church. (3) Christological transposition: where the original psalm may have described Moses ascending Sinai and receiving the law, or God ascending Zion and receiving worship, Paul sees the greater fulfillment: the Son ascends to the Father, receives all authority (Philippians 2:9–11; Acts 2:33), and from that position of exaltation pours gifts upon his people. The Spirit given at Pentecost (Acts 2:33: “having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this”) is precisely the dynamic Paul is invoking. The adaptation is typologically and theologically grounded, not textually careless.

verseByVerse.quote: (In saying, 'He ascended,' what does it mean but that he had also descended into the lower regions, the earth? He who descended is the one who also ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s parenthetical commentary addresses a logical implication: ascent presupposes prior descent. The eternal Son descended — into the humiliation of incarnation, into the full depth of human experience, into death itself. The one who went down is the one who went up. The descent and ascent together span the entire vertical range of existence, so that the ascended Christ might “fill all things” — permeate all of reality with his presence, lordship, and life-giving power. There is no depth of human suffering where Christ has not gone and from which he has not returned in triumph. Sproul: “There is no place in the universe, no depth of human experience, where Christ has not gone — and from which he has not returned victorious.”

‘The lower parts of the earth’ has been read in two main ways, and both are worth knowing. Most modern Reformed scholars take it to mean the earth itself — “the lower parts, namely the earth” — so the descent is the Incarnation: the eternal Son left heaven and came down to earth. This makes the contrast beautifully simple: heaven above, earth below, ascent out of the place he had entered. The other reading, going back to Chrysostom, Origen, and the tradition behind the Apostles’ Creed (“he descended into hell”), takes “lower parts of the earth” to mean below the earth — the realm of the dead — so that the descent includes Christ’s death and his going to the place of the dead before the resurrection (cf. Psalm 63:9; 1 Peter 3:18–20). Either reading makes the same theological point: Christ’s exaltation to the highest place presupposes his willingness to descend to the lowest. The one who now fills all things is the one who first emptied himself of glory to enter our world. This is the inexhaustible wonder of the Incarnation.

“That he might fill all things” — hina plērōsē ta panta — is one of the most majestic phrases in this entire letter, and it is not a stray thought. The word plērō (to fill, to bring to fullness) and its cognates course through Ephesians like a great river. In 1:23 the church is “the fullness of him who fills all in all.” In 3:19 Paul prays that believers might “be filled with all the fullness of God.” In 4:13 the goal of every gift is “the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.” In 5:18 the imperative is “be filled with the Spirit.” This is not coincidence — it is the theological pulse of the letter. Paul is telling us that the mission of the ascended Christ is the progressive filling of all creation with his glory, his presence, his life.

What does it mean that Christ fills all things? It means he is not absent from any corner of his universe. He who descended to the lowest depth and ascended to the highest height now holds all of reality in the span of his sovereign presence. He fills the cosmos as Lord. He fills the church as Head. He fills each believer by his Spirit. This is not pantheism — Christ does not become creation — but it is something astonishing: the exalted God-man, bearing a glorified human nature, exercises a universal lordship and presence that leaves nothing outside his reach. Creation groans for this fullness (Rom. 8:22). The church is being built toward this fullness. History is moving toward the moment when the filling is complete and God is “all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28). cf. Col. 1:17–20; Eph. 1:22–23.

For the preacher and the struggling saint alike, this is breathtaking comfort. There is no situation so empty of hope, no life so hollowed out by grief or sin or loss, that the filling Christ cannot enter it. He who filled the far country of death now fills the far country of your suffering. The one who fills all things has not overlooked you.

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are not spiritual gifts as such — they are gifted persons given to the church. Christ gives people as gifts. Notice: apostles and prophets are listed first (cf. 2:20 — the foundation), then the continuing offices of evangelist and pastor-teacher. The Greek construction suggests “shepherds and teachers” may be a single office — the pastor who teaches.

The Apostles were those personally commissioned by the risen Christ, eyewitnesses of the resurrection, with authority to speak and write his word with binding force. Paul lists himself in this category despite not having walked with Jesus during his ministry (1 Cor. 9:1; 15:8). Their role was foundational and unrepeatable: the New Testament is their legacy. The church is “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. 2:20) — a foundation is laid once. There are no apostles today in this primary sense.

The Prophets here are New Testament prophets, not the great writing prophets of the Old Testament. They received and declared direct revelation from the Spirit, filling in the teaching of the church before the canon was complete (cf. Acts 11:27–28; 13:1–2). Alongside the apostles they belong to the foundational era. With the closing of the canon their revelatory function ceased, though the gift of proclamation — forthtelling rather than foretelling — continues in every preacher who opens the word.

The Evangelists were those especially gifted and called to carry the gospel to those who had not yet heard it — travelling proclaimers of Christ, like Philip (Acts 21:8) and Timothy (2 Tim. 4:5). Their work is not confined to the apostolic age. Wherever the gospel frontier advances, Christ gives evangelists. They are frontier workers: breaking ground, planting churches, moving on. The church needs them in every generation.

The Shepherds and Teachers (literally poimenas kai didaskalous) are almost certainly a single office, as the Greek article groups them together. This is the pastor-teacher: the one who tends the flock by feeding it the word. The shepherd image stresses care, protection, and knowing the sheep by name (cf. John 10:11–14; 1 Peter 5:1–4); the teacher image stresses the means by which that care is exercised — systematic, faithful, nourishing exposition of Scripture. Where the apostle laid the foundation and the evangelist broke new ground, the pastor-teacher builds up what remains — steadily, patiently, week by week, over a lifetime.

PREACHER’S NOTE Sproul and MacArthur both note that the foundational offices of apostle and prophet were tied to the completion of the canon; the continuing offices are evangelist and pastor-teacher. The church is still built today by those who preach the word. Every pastor stands in this long line of gifted persons whom Christ himself has given to his church. That is both a humbling and a glorious calling.

verseByVerse.quote: to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the most transformative verses in ecclesiology. The purpose of the gifted leaders is not to do the ministry for the saints but to equip (katartismon — the word used for mending nets, setting bones: fitting something for its proper function) the saints so that they do the work of ministry. The building up of the body is the saints’ work, under Word-shaped leadership.

The practical implication is staggering: a healthy church is not one where a gifted minister does everything, but one where the whole body is equipped and active. Pastoral ministry is not performance; it is preparation (cf. Rom. 12:4–5; 1 Cor. 12:7).

How are the saints equipped? Paul does not leave this vague. Each of the four offices of verse 11 equips in its own way, together forming a complete environment of formation:

  • Through the apostles — the saints are equipped by the apostolic writings: the New Testament Scriptures, which carry the full weight of Christ’s own authority. Every time the word is opened and preached, the apostles are still equipping the church. The canon is not a closed archive; it is a living instrument.
  • Through the prophets — the saints are equipped by the whole counsel of God’s word, Old and New Testament, which the prophetic tradition gave us. Proclamation that opens this word — applying it to conscience, rebuking sin, stirring hope — is the prophetic voice still at work in the pulpit.
  • Through the evangelist — the saints are equipped not only by hearing the gospel but by seeing it preached and learning to share it themselves. A healthy evangelist does not merely win converts; he trains the congregation to be witnesses in their own households, workplaces, and neighbourhoods.
  • Through the pastor-teacher — the saints are equipped by systematic, patient, week-by-week feeding of the word: doctrine that shapes the mind, exhortation that moves the will, and pastoral care that tends individual souls. This is the slow work of katartismō — mending, fitting, maturing — applied person by person, year by year.

The result Paul envisions is a congregation of ministers, not a minister with a congregation. Every member fitted for their function. Every joint contributing (v. 16). This is the church in full health.

What kind of ministry can members do? Paul uses the broad word diakonia — service — deliberately. It is not restricted to pulpit or platform. The New Testament fills in the picture richly:

  • Serving and practical care — meeting practical needs: feeding the hungry, visiting the sick, caring for widows, welcoming the stranger (Matt. 25:35–36; Rom. 12:13; James 1:27). This is ministry as much as preaching.
  • Encouragement and exhortation — speaking words that strengthen faith, comfort the grieving, and call the wandering back (Heb. 3:13; 1 Thess. 5:11). Every believer can do this.
  • Teaching and discipling — instructing others in the faith, whether formally in a small group or informally one-to-one (Col. 3:16; 2 Tim. 2:2; Titus 2:3–5). Older saints teaching younger. Fathers and mothers teaching children.
  • Evangelism and witness — telling neighbours, colleagues, and family about Christ. Not everyone is an evangelist by office, but every member is a witness by calling (Acts 1:8; 1 Peter 3:15).
  • Prayer — intercession for one another, for the church, for the lost, for rulers (Eph. 6:18; 1 Tim. 2:1). Prayer is not the least of ministries; it may be the most powerful.
  • Giving — the ministry of generous, joyful giving that funds gospel work and sustains those in need (2 Cor. 9:6–8; Phil. 4:17–18). Generosity is a form of building the body.

No gift is too small and no calling too ordinary to be included in diakonia. The woman who quietly visits the lonely widow, the man who opens his home for a small group, the teenager who shares the gospel with a classmate — all are doing the work of ministry. Christ gave the gifted leaders so that this becomes every member’s normal life.

What does “building up the body of Christ” mean? The image is architectural — oikodomē, the construction of a building (cf. 2:21–22 where the church is a temple being built). But the building is alive: it is a body, and it grows. Paul holds both images in tension deliberately, because no single metaphor is large enough for what the church is.

Building up the body means at least three things working together:

  • Numerical growth — new members added as the lost are converted and welcomed in. The body grows by addition. Evangelism is not optional; it is part of the building project (cf. Acts 2:47).
  • Maturity and depth — each existing member growing in knowledge, faith, love, and Christlikeness (vv. 13–15). A church can grow numerically and still be immature — Paul’s concern here is primarily that the body reaches “mature manhood, the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (v. 13). This happens through the word, prayer, suffering, and the mutual ministry of members to one another.
  • Unity and cohesion — the joints being fitted, the parts working properly together (v. 16). A body that is growing but fragmented is not healthy. Love is the mortar (v. 16b). Building up the body always has a corporate, relational dimension: you cannot build the body by yourself, alone.

Ultimately, building up the body of Christ is participating in the very purpose of God for history. The church is not a social club that God happens to approve of; it is “the fullness of him who fills all in all” (1:23). To serve one another faithfully in the smallest act of diakonia is to contribute to something of eternal and cosmic significance.

verseByVerse.quote: until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, so that we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro by the waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine, by human cunning, by craftiness in deceitful schemes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The goal is eschatological as well as present: maturity is a direction of travel. Tēlikia — the full stature, the complete measure of Christ. The contrast in verse 14 is between children tossed at sea and mature adults standing firm. False teaching is the wind; doctrinal depth is the anchor. The solution to theological instability is not suspicion but growth — growing up into Christ through the ministry of the Word.

Paul stacks four phrases here, each one deepening the picture of where all this equipping and ministry is meant to lead. They are not four separate destinations but four angles on a single glorious goal.

“The unity of the faith” — this is not the unity of tolerance, where differences are smoothed over by indifference to truth. It is the unity that comes when the whole body holds the same faith — the apostolic deposit, the gospel received, the confession shared. The article is important: the faith, not merely a personal believing. As the church grows in understanding of what it believes together, division and faction give way to a deep, joyful agreement rooted in the word. This unity is not already fully achieved; it is the direction every sermon, every small group, every act of mutual teaching is aimed at. cf. Jude 3; Phil. 1:27.

“The knowledge of the Son of God” — the Greek is epignōsis, not mere intellectual acquaintance but full, personal, experiential knowing — the kind of knowing that transforms the knower. This is knowledge of a Person, not merely knowledge of a doctrine. The Son of God is not a topic to master but a Lord to know ever more deeply. Calvin wrote that the whole of the Christian life is a progressive knowing of Christ — and that we are never so advanced that we do not need to know him better. The goal of all Christian ministry is not a more informed congregation but a congregation more deeply captivated by Jesus Christ himself.

“Mature manhood” — andra teleion, a complete or perfect man. Paul speaks corporately: the whole church together reaching the maturity of a fully-grown person. Individually, every believer is to leave behind the instability and gullibility of spiritual infancy and reach the settled, rooted, discerning character of an adult. Maturity here is not the absence of struggle but the presence of stability — a faith that is no longer easily capsized. It involves theological depth, moral seriousness, and the relational wisdom to speak truth in love (v. 15). It is what the years of faithful preaching, suffering, prayer, and community are meant to produce.

“The measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” — the most breathtaking phrase of the four. The standard of maturity is not a human benchmark — not the most admirable elder in your congregation, not some abstract ideal of virtue. It is Christ himself in his fullness. Plērōma again — the fullness that fills all things (v. 10), that the church is called to embody (1:23). Paul is saying: the destination is nothing less than the church collectively reflecting the full character, wisdom, love, and glory of Jesus Christ. This will not be fully achieved until the last day — it is an eschatological goal — but it is the real goal, not a figure of speech. Every act of ministry, every word of encouragement, every prayer, every sermon is a small contribution to this staggering end: a people who, together, look like Christ.

PREACHER’S NOTE “Cunning” in v. 14 translates panourgia — craftiness, the word used of the serpent in Genesis. Doctrinal deception has always employed theological-sounding language. The antidote is always the same: deep knowledge of the Son of God. Show your congregation not merely why false teaching is dangerous, but how knowing Christ more deeply is the only lasting defence.

verseByVerse.quote: Rather, speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and held together by every joint with which it is equipped, when each part is working properly, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Alētheuontes en agapē — truthing in love. Not just speaking truth but living it, embodying it, in a context of love. Truth without love is cold; love without truth is hollow. The maturing church holds both together as it grows into its head.

What truth did Paul have in mind? The context supplies the answer. The preceding verses speak of the apostolic faith (v. 13), the knowledge of the Son of God (v. 13), and the danger of being swept away by false doctrine (v. 14). The truth Paul means is above all the gospel truth — the content of the faith: who Christ is, what he has done, what it means to live in him. It is theological and moral truth together: the truth about God, about humanity, about sin and grace and the new life. It is the truth that the wolves of verse 14 are trying to distort. And it is truth that must be spoken — in preaching, in correction, in personal conversation, in the daily witness of a life aligned with the gospel. Stott writes: “Christians are to be truth-speakers. This has to do with what comes out of our mouths in the company of fellow believers and in the world.” cf. Col. 3:16; 2 Tim. 4:2.

What did “in love” mean? Not primarily “in a nice tone of voice” — though gentleness matters (2 Tim. 2:25). The love Paul has in mind is something deeper and more demanding than pleasantness. It is love with a goal: the good of the other person, the health of the body, the glory of Christ. It means speaking truth for someone rather than at them. It means the motive is not to win an argument, protect a reputation, or score a theological point, but to build up. Love is what separates the surgeon’s scalpel from the bully’s fist — both may cause pain, but only one is aimed at healing. Proverbs 27:6 captures it: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy.” And Galatians 4:16, where Paul asks with grief: “Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?” Truth told in love is costly to the speaker. It risks the relationship for the sake of the person.

“Grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ” — the phrase “in every way” is important. Paul does not allow partial growth. It is not enough to grow in knowledge while love withers, or to grow in zeal while wisdom lags. The call is comprehensive: in doctrine, in character, in relationships, in worship, in witness, in suffering — in all of it, the direction is the same: into Christ. He is not merely the model of maturity; he is the substance of it. To grow up is not to become more impressive versions of ourselves; it is to become more like him, more hidden in him, more fully shaped by his mind and heart. The head gives direction to the whole body — Christ’s lordship over every dimension of the church’s life is what Paul is after. Nothing is exempt. No corner of the church’s life, no part of a believer’s character, is permitted to stay immature. cf. Col. 2:19; 2 Cor. 3:18.

Verse 16 is a masterpiece of organic metaphor: Christ is the head from whom the whole body is joined and held together by every supporting ligament, each part working properly, growing the body in love. The church’s health depends on connection to Christ, on the proper working of every member, and on love as the animating principle. MacArthur calls this “the most comprehensive description of church growth in the New Testament.”

“Makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love” — what did Paul mean? All three things you might intuit are present, and Paul intends them together:

  • More mature — this is the primary thrust in context. The body grows toward the fullness of Christ (v. 13). Each member, as their part works properly, draws the whole body further from the immaturity of verse 14 and closer to the settled, Christ-shaped wholeness of verse 13. Growth here is deepening: richer doctrine, stronger faith, more Christlike character, more stable love.
  • More loving — love is named as both the means and the end: the body builds itself up in love. This is the same love that grounds unity in verses 1–3, that governs truth-speaking in verse 15, and that will characterise every practical command in verses 25–32. As the body matures it does not simply become more theologically precise; it becomes more warm, more patient, more self-giving. Maturity without growing love is not maturity — it is merely sophistication.
  • Larger in number — Paul almost certainly has numerical growth in view as well. A body that is “working properly” includes the evangelist of verse 11 and the witnessing members of verse 12. A healthy organism grows outward as well as inward. As the body is built up in love, it becomes attractive to the world — Jesus said as much: “By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). A church overflowing with the love described here is itself an instrument of evangelism.

What does this look like in practice? Paul’s image of joints and ligaments is deliberately concrete. He is not describing a mystical experience but an organic, structural reality. In practice, the self-building body looks like this:

  • The member with the gift of encouragement seeks out the one who is struggling and speaks life into them — a joint doing its work.
  • The small group that studies the word together, prays honestly, and holds each other accountable — ligaments holding the body together under pressure.
  • The older woman who takes time to disciple a younger one in how to love her husband and raise her children (Titus 2:3–5) — a part working properly.
  • The congregation that disagrees over a secondary matter and chooses to absorb the cost rather than fracture — the bond of peace (v. 3) holding under strain.
  • The deacon who visits the sick, the giver who funds the missionary, the intercessor who rises early to pray for the church — all of them building, all of them contributing to growth.

None of this is spectacular. Most of it is invisible. That is precisely Paul’s point: the body grows not through the heroics of a few outstanding individuals but through the faithful, ordinary, daily contribution of every part. The ligament is never seen. The joint is never applauded. But remove them and the body collapses. Every quiet act of service, every honest conversation, every prayer offered for a fellow member — these are the materials from which Christ is building his church. cf. 1 Cor. 12:21–26; Col. 2:19.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Put Off the Old, Put On the New
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"No longer walk as the Gentiles walk." The second great imperative of the practical section opens a window on the human condition apart from God, and what Paul shows us is not a flattering picture. The Gentile walk — the life lived without the knowledge and presence of God — is characterized by futility of mind, darkened understanding, hardness of heart, and the abandonment of moral restraint in the pursuit of every kind of impurity with insatiable craving. This is not a description of particularly depraved people; it is a description of the natural trajectory of a life lived in alienation from God. When the connection to the source of light is severed, the mind darkens. When the conscience is repeatedly ignored, the heart hardens. When human beings make themselves the centre of their own moral universe, desire loses its proper objects and becomes insatiable.

But the Ephesians have not learned Christ that way. If they have truly heard Him and been taught in Him — as the truth is in Jesus — then they have received something that changes everything: a new self. Not a reformed version of the old self, not the old self disciplined into better behaviour, but a genuinely new creation — created in the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness. Between the old self and the new stands the renewing of the mind: the ongoing transformation of the interior world of thought, desire, imagination, and perception. The mind that has been renewed by the Spirit perceives reality differently, desires differently, and therefore lives differently.

Paul's language here is the language of clothing: put off, put on. The old self is like a garment — something worn, something that can be removed. The new self is the garment appropriate to who you now are in Christ. The metaphor implies both decision and daily practice: the decision to stop wearing what belongs to the old life, and the daily discipline of putting on what belongs to the new. Sanctification is not passive; it requires the active cooperation of the will with the Spirit who is doing the renewing.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Renewal of the Mind and the New Humanity

The "old self" and "new self" of this passage are not psychological categories — they are eschatological ones. The old self is the Adamic humanity: the self that has inherited Adam's corruption, lives under the dominion of sin, and is "corrupt through deceitful desires" (v.22). The new self is the new humanity created in Christ — what Paul elsewhere calls "the last Adam" (1 Corinthians 15:45). To be "in Christ" is to have been transferred from the old humanity to the new, from the domain of the first Adam to the domain of the Second.

The renewing of the mind (v.23) is the cognitive dimension of this transfer. Romans 12:2 makes the same point: "be transformed by the renewal of your mind." The mind that has been shaped by the world — its values, its assumptions, its desires — must be reshaped by the word and Spirit of God. This is not achieved in a moment; it is the work of a lifetime. Every act of sustained Bible meditation, every time truth displaces a lie, every time a Spirit-given desire overcomes a flesh-driven one, the mind is being renewed. This is the slow and glorious work of sanctification.

The goal of the renewal is "the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (v.24). This is the restoration of the image of God that was defaced at the fall. God made humanity in His image; sin corrupted that image; Christ has come to restore it. The new self is not merely morally better than the old — it is ontologically different, created anew after the very likeness of God. This is why the Christian life is not ultimately about rule-keeping but about becoming who you already are in Christ: the image-bearer of God, restored and renewed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ephesus was a city of extraordinary sensual abundance. The temple complex of Artemis, the bath-houses, the theatre, the commercial district — pleasure was available in every form and at every price. To be a Christian in Ephesus was to swim against a powerful and relentless current. Paul does not tell the Ephesian Christians to try harder or to exercise greater willpower. He gives them something more powerful: a new identity. You are not the old self anymore. The garment of the old life is to be put off — not held on to, not worn occasionally for old time's sake, but removed and discarded. And in its place: the new self, created after God's own likeness.

Now: The pornified, entertainment-saturated, hyper-stimulated culture of the 21st century is Ephesus with better technology. The mechanisms of desire-manipulation are more sophisticated; the availability of darkness is more immediate; the cultural current against a holy life runs faster. Paul's answer is unchanged and still the most powerful available: not more discipline applied to the old self, but the daily renewal of the mind in the truth of the gospel — who you are in Christ, what you have been given, who you are becoming. The Christian who meditates daily on Scripture, who submits their thinking to the word of God, who asks the Spirit to renew their mind — this person is not swimming against the current on their own. They are being transformed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this I say and testify in the Lord, that you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their minds.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul frames the ethical turn with apostolic solemnity: “I say and testify in the Lord.” This is not personal preference but Spirit-authorised command. The contrast is stark: they were Gentiles; now, in Christ, they must live differently. The root of Gentile lostness is intellectual: “futility of their minds” (mataiotēti tou noos) — vain, empty, purposeless thinking, unmoored from God and drifting toward unreality. Romans 1:21 traces the same diagnosis: “their thinking became futile.” The ethical collapse described in vv. 18–19 grows from this intellectual root.

verseByVerse.quote: They are darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart. They have become callous and have given themselves up to sensuality, greedy to practice every kind of impurity.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul traces the anatomy of moral ruin in four linked stages: hardness of heart (the root) → ignorance → alienation from the life of God → sensuality and insatiable impurity (the fruit). “Darkened in their understanding” does not mean intellectual incompetence but moral blindness — the inability to see God, self, and others truly. “Hardness of heart” (pōrōsis) is the calcification of the will against God; it is not merely passive but the result of repeated rejection. “Given themselves up” echoes Romans 1 — God does not arbitrarily abandon but releases people into the trajectory they have chosen. The end is not freedom but insatiable appetite: “greedy” (en pleonexia) — craving that cannot be satisfied.

verseByVerse.quote: But that is not the way you learned Christ! — assuming that you have heard about him and were taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary: One of Paul’s most electrifying phrases: “you learned Christ” — not learned about Christ. He is not merely a subject of instruction; he is the content of the learning itself. To be taught “in him” is to enter a living relationship with a teacher who is also the truth. “As the truth is in Jesus” — Paul uses the human name deliberately. The doctrinal content and the historical person are inseparable: there is no abstract Christian ethics floating free from the incarnate, crucified, risen Lord who walked in Galilee. The contrast with the futile Gentile mind (v. 17) could not be sharper: reality is found only in him.

verseByVerse.quote: to put off your old self, which belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Put off” draws on the image of stripping old garments — not merely bad habits but the entire identity and orientation of the pre-conversion self. The “old self” is the whole human being oriented toward created things rather than the Creator. It is “corrupt through deceitful desires” — the old self is in a state of ongoing deterioration, aging and rotting toward death. Desires that promise satisfaction deliver only corruption; cravings that lie about what they can give. This self must be stripped off entirely, not patched or improved.

But how, in practice, does a Christian actually put off the old self? This is the question every honest believer asks. The command is clear; the method feels elusive. Scripture gives concrete, practicable guidance.

1. Recognise that the old self is already crucified. Romans 6:6 says “our old self was crucified with him.” The old self is not an enemy at full strength; it is a defeated power still making noise. You are not trying to kill something by willpower alone; you are refusing to live as though something dead were still alive. The first act of putting off is a theological one — believing what God declares is true: the old self has no rightful claim on you any more. cf. Rom. 6:11: “consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God.”

2. Name the specific pattern, not just the general problem. Paul does this himself in verses 25–31: not “put off dishonesty” in the abstract, but “put away falsehood” and “speak truth with your neighbour.” In practice: what specific thought pattern, appetite, or behaviour belongs to the old self in your life right now? Anger? Lust? Pride? Self-pity? Envy? A particular sin named and brought into the light loses the cover of darkness. Unconfessed and unnamed, it rules. cf. James 5:16; 1 John 1:9.

3. Starve the old pattern — do not feed what you want to kill. Romans 13:14: “make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires.” Remove the inputs that feed the old pattern. This may mean closing a screen, ending a conversation, avoiding a place, or restructuring a routine. The person who prays for purity and keeps their phone on the bedside table at night is asking God to defeat an enemy they are still feeding. Spiritual warfare is often surprisingly practical.

4. Put on, do not merely put off. Paul’s grammar is a threefold movement: put off — be renewed — put on. A house swept clean but left empty is vulnerable (Matt. 12:44). For every old pattern identified, ask: what is the corresponding new self behaviour I must cultivate? Replace bitterness with active forgiveness. Replace lying with deliberate truth-telling. Replace idle consumption with purposeful Scripture meditation. The old pattern must be displaced, not merely suppressed. Paul gives five specific put-off / put-on pairs in verses 25–32.

5. Renew the mind daily. Verse 23 sits at the centre of the three commands deliberately: “be renewed in the spirit of your minds.” The old self is fed by old thinking; it collapses when the mind is retrained. In practice: daily, unhurried immersion in Scripture — not for information but for transformation. Honest prayer that names the specific temptation. Sermons received as word from God, not performance to evaluate. The renewed mind is not achieved in a crisis moment; it is the fruit of sustained daily discipline. cf. Rom. 12:2; Ps. 119:11.

6. Do not fight alone. The old self thrives in isolation. Hebrews 3:13: “exhort one another every day… that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.” Find one or two believers who know the specific struggle, who will ask the hard question and pray with you. The Christian life is designed for community, and putting off the old self is no exception.

The putting off is a lifelong discipline, not a single event. There will be days when the old garment seems to go back on almost without noticing. That is not a sign grace has failed; it is the normal texture of sanctification in a fallen body. The answer is not despair but return: confess, believe, put off again, put on again, be renewed again. And the one who began this good work is faithful to complete it (Phil. 1:6).

verseByVerse.quote: and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds, and to put on the new self, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three infinitives structure the moral renewal: put off (v. 22) — be renewed (v. 23) — put on (v. 24). The middle term is the hinge: “be renewed” (ananeousthai, present passive) is an ongoing renewal by the Spirit working in the deepest part of the person. The “new self” (kainon anthrōpon) is not self-constructed but created — the same word as in 2:10. This new humanity is created “after the likeness of God,” recovering the image of Genesis 1:26–27 as restored in Christ. “True righteousness and holiness” — not religious performance but the genuine reality of a life conformed to God’s own character. Stott: “The new man is not the old man improved, but a new creation.”

But how does the Christian actually experience this renewal? The grammar is the first clue: ananeousthai is present passive — continuous and received, not achieved. This is not something you do by effort; it is something done to you, by the Spirit, as you place yourself in the path of his working. The distinction is vital. God is the agent of renewal; the Christian is the recipient. But Scripture is equally clear that God works through means — and the Christian must actively, deliberately make use of those means. Passivity is not the same as receptivity.

How God works: Renewal is the Spirit’s sovereign work in the innermost person. He illuminates the mind to see Christ as glorious (2 Cor. 3:18; 4:6). He convicts of sin and draws the will toward repentance (John 16:8). He conforms the believer progressively to the image of Christ from one degree of glory to another (2 Cor. 3:18). He intercedes within the believer with groanings too deep for words (Rom. 8:26). None of this is earned or manufactured. It is sheer grace, the continuing work of the same Spirit who raised Christ from the dead. The Christian does not produce renewal; the Christian receives it.

What the Christian does — the means of renewal:

  • Scripture — feed the new mind its proper food. The Spirit renews through the word (John 17:17: “sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth”). Daily, attentive reading is not a duty to perform but a meal to eat. The mind is renewed as it is soaked in how God thinks — about himself, about humanity, about sin, about grace, about what is truly valuable. A Christian who neglects Scripture is starving the very faculty meant to be renewed. cf. Ps. 119:9; Col. 3:16.
  • Prayer — ask for what only God can give. Paul prays for this renewal in Ephesians 3:16: “that he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being.” The Christian who prays specifically — “Lord, renew my thinking about this; give me the mind of Christ here” — is not performing a ritual but acknowledging that renewal is a gift and asking the Giver for it. cf. Phil. 4:6–7, where the peace that “guards the mind” comes through prayer.
  • The preached word — receive it as word from God, not word about God. The congregation gathered around faithful preaching is not an audience watching a performance; it is a people being addressed by the living God through his servant. 1 Thessalonians 2:13: “you received it not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God, which is at work in you believers.” The renewed mind is formed week by week as Scripture is opened and received with faith.
  • Suffering and trials — embrace the school you did not choose. Romans 5:3–4 traces the path: suffering produces endurance, endurance character, character hope. Trials do what comfortable circumstances cannot: they expose what the old self is still clinging to and drive the mind back to what is truly solid. The Christian who receives hardship as from a sovereign Father finds that God uses it as one of his sharpest tools of renewal. cf. James 1:2–4; Heb. 12:10–11.
  • Christian community — be shaped by the body. Hebrews 10:24–25 calls believers to “stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together.” The honest word from a friend, the example of someone further along the path, the accountability of a small group — these are not additions to renewal; they are part of its ordinary means. cf. Prov. 27:17.
  • Obedience — act on what you know, and the knowing deepens. John 7:17: “if anyone’s will is to do God’s will, he will know.” Renewal is not only prior to obedience; it is deepened by obedience. The Christian who acts on what Scripture says — even imperfectly, even reluctantly — finds their mind further shaped by the act. Obedience is itself a means of grace. The mind that chooses truth again and again gradually finds truth more natural and the old patterns less compelling.

The Christian life is therefore neither pure passivity (“let go and let God”) nor sheer willpower (“try harder”). It is what theologians call the “means of grace”: deliberate, sustained use of the channels through which the Spirit works. You cannot renew yourself. But you can place yourself, daily and repeatedly, in the hands of the One who can. That is what it means to be renewed in the spirit of your minds. cf. 2 Cor. 3:18; Phil. 2:12–13.

“Put on the new self” — what does this actually mean? If putting off is the stripping away of the old identity and its patterns, putting on is the active, deliberate clothing of the self in a new one. The verb is again an imperative — not a passive waiting for the new self to appear, but a conscious act of faith: reckon yourself to be who God says you are, and live accordingly. It is the same logic as Romans 13:14: “put on the Lord Jesus Christ.” To put on the new self is to put on Christ — to act from his identity rather than the old one, to let his character be the clothes you wear into every room, every relationship, every decision. In practice it means asking in any given moment: what would the new self — the person I am in Christ — do here? And then doing that, by faith, before the feeling follows.

“Created after the likeness of God” — this phrase reaches all the way back to Genesis 1:26–27, where humanity was made in the image and likeness of God. That image was defaced but not destroyed by the fall; it is now being restored, and more than restored, in Christ. The new self is not a patched-up version of the old; it is a new creation (2 Cor. 5:17), bearing the family likeness of God himself. This is staggering: the goal of the Christian life is not moral improvement but the recovery of the divine image — thinking God’s thoughts, loving what God loves, hating what God hates, relating to others with God’s own character written into the grain of the soul. cf. Col. 3:10: “renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator.”

“In true righteousness and holiness” — Paul distinguishes two dimensions of this restored image:

  • Righteousness (dikaiosynē) points to right relating — to God and to others. It is the character of a person who gives to God and to neighbour what is truly owed: worship, honour, truth, justice, love. It covers the whole relational fabric of life. The righteous person is not merely law-abiding; they are rightly ordered in every relationship.
  • Holiness (hosiotēs) points to consecration — a life set apart for God, devoted to him, marked by reverence and purity. Where righteousness looks outward to relationships, holiness looks upward to God. Together they cover the whole of the new self’s character: right before God, right before people.

The word “true” (alēthinais) is significant. Paul is contrasting this with the counterfeit versions — the righteousness of the Pharisee that is performance without inward reality, the religious observance that is outward conformity without love for God. The new self is not a better mask; it is a new heart. What the law demanded and the old self could never deliver, the new self embodies — not perfectly yet, but genuinely, and progressively more so as the Spirit does his renewing work. This is the destination of all the putting off, all the renewal, all the putting on: a person who is truly, inwardly, growing into the image of God in Christ — and who will one day, when they see him as he is, be fully conformed to that image at last (1 John 3:2).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The abstract imperatives of the previous section now descend into the daily texture of community life with startling specificity. Paul gives five concrete commands — truthful speech, controlled anger, honest work, building words, and radical forgiveness — and each one carries a reason attached to it, and every reason is a reason drawn from the gospel. This is characteristic of Paul's ethical method: he never says merely "do this." He says "do this because of what Christ has done, because of who you are in Him, because of the Spirit who lives in you." The ethics are embedded in the theology; the imperative is always clothed in grace.

The command about anger is worth particular attention: "Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil" (vv.26–27). Paul does not say "do not be angry." He says be angry and do not sin. Anger is not automatically sinful; there are things worth being angry about, and the person who feels no anger at injustice or sin has a problem. But anger that is nursed, that is carried through the night, that is allowed to harden into bitterness and resentment — this anger gives the devil a foothold. It creates a space in the community for the adversary to work. The practical implication: move toward resolution, always. The direction of the Christian community is always toward reconciliation.

The governing principle of the whole section is verse 30: do not grieve the Holy Spirit. The Spirit is not a theological abstraction; He is a Person who can be grieved, whose presence is sensitive to the moral atmosphere of the community He inhabits. The practical holiness Paul calls for in these verses is not primarily about rule-keeping; it is about maintaining an environment in which the Spirit of God is at home, in which His presence and power can flow freely through the community. And the final verse draws the standard: forgive one another as God in Christ forgave you. The cross is the measure. Nothing less.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Grieving of the Spirit and the Ethics of Grace

Verse 30 — "do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption" — is one of the most searching statements in the New Testament about the nature of the Spirit. He can be grieved. This word (lupeō) in Greek means to cause sorrow, to wound. The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal force that responds mechanically to human sin; He is a Person with genuine emotional sensibility who is affected by the moral life of the community He inhabits. The sins Paul has listed — falsehood, uncontrolled anger, stealing, corrupting speech, bitterness, wrath, malice — do not merely harm the community; they wound the indwelling Guest.

The phrase "by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption" provides the context for the warning. The Spirit who can be grieved is the same Spirit who has sealed us for the final day — who is our guarantee of the inheritance (1:14), the deposit of our future glory. To grieve Him is therefore not a trivial matter; it is to harm the very relationship that is the ground of our assurance and the means of our transformation. This is not a threat to the believer's salvation; Paul does not say "by whom you were sealed unless you grieve Him." The sealing is certain. But the quality of the Spirit's presence and work in the community is affected by how the community lives.

The climactic command — "forgive one another, as God in Christ forgave you" (v.32) — sets the standard for Christian forgiveness at the level of the cross: freely given, fully extended, without conditions. The Reformers consistently emphasised that forgiveness is not a feeling but a decision — the decision to release the debt, to no longer hold the offence against the offender, to treat them as God treats us in Christ: with kindness and grace. This is impossible from human resources. It is possible only for those who have received it from God and draw on the same source to extend it to others.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Ephesian church was, as we have noted, extraordinarily diverse. With diversity comes friction. The command against falsehood (v.25) — "speak truth with your neighbour, for we are members of one another" — addresses the social lubricant of deception that holds many human communities together. In the body of Christ, truth-telling is not optional; it is structurally necessary. A body in which the members lie to one another cannot function. The command against corrupting speech (v.29) — only what builds up — addresses the tongue that tears down, the word that diminishes, the comment that cuts. In a diverse community under pressure, these are the sins most likely to do lasting damage.

Now: "Do not let the sun go down on your anger" is one of the most practically demanding commands in Scripture, and one of the most consistently violated in married life, family life, and church life. We carry grievances. We nurse wounds. We let distance harden into walls. The apostle's word cuts through all of it: move toward resolution before night falls. This does not mean every conflict is resolved in an evening — some wounds take weeks of patient, humble work to heal. But the direction must always be toward each other, not away. The community that actually practices this — that refuses to let resentment calcify, that keeps short accounts, that forgives as God in Christ forgave — will be noticed. It will be extraordinary. It will be a sign of the Kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ethical imperatives now flow from the theological reality. Truth-telling is the most basic social act of the new community. Paul grounds it ecclesially: “for we are members of one another.” Lying to a fellow believer is self-harm — we are the same body. The lie corrodes the trust that makes communal life possible.

What did Paul mean by “falsehood”? The Greek pseudos covers the full range of untruth — not only outright lies but every form of communication designed to create a false impression: half-truths that mislead, silence that conceals what should be said, flattery that says what people want to hear rather than what is true, exaggeration that distorts, and the careful management of reputation that presents a better self than actually exists. Falsehood is not only a moral failure; Paul has already shown (vv. 17–19) that it belongs to the old self — the life unmoored from God, built on unreality, drifting toward corruption. To continue in falsehood after putting on the new self is to dress in new clothes and then reach back for the old rags.

In practice, the falsehood Paul has in mind includes:

  • Direct lying — saying what you know to be untrue, whether to protect yourself, avoid conflict, or gain advantage.
  • Deceptive framing — telling technically true things in a way deliberately designed to mislead: selecting facts, omitting context, letting a false inference stand uncorrected.
  • Flattery and people-pleasing — saying what will make someone feel good rather than what is true and helpful (cf. Prov. 29:5; Gal. 1:10). This is one of the subtlest and most common forms of falsehood in Christian community.
  • Silence when truth is required — failing to speak a necessary word of correction, warning, or honest feedback because it is uncomfortable. Omission can be as dishonest as commission.
  • Image management — carefully curating how others perceive you; presenting a more spiritual, more competent, or more together version of yourself than is real. This is falsehood directed at the community as a whole.

What did Paul mean by “speak the truth with his neighbour”? The word “neighbour” (plēsion) echoes Zechariah 8:16, which Paul is quoting: “speak the truth to one another.” In its Old Testament context this was a call to covenant faithfulness within the community of God’s people. Paul inherits that weight and applies it to the church. Speaking the truth means more than not lying; it means being the kind of person in whose mouth others can place full trust — whose yes means yes, whose counsel is honest, who will say the difficult thing when it needs to be said, and who says it not to wound but to serve. It includes:

  • Honest speech in everyday conversation — meaning what you say, saying what you mean, keeping your word in small things as in large.
  • Speaking truthfully about yourself — not projecting false spirituality or competence; being willing to say “I was wrong,” “I don’t know,” “I am struggling.”
  • Honest pastoral speech — giving the honest word when a friend is making a serious mistake, even when silence would be easier. This is the truth-in-love of verse 15 applied to the daily life of the congregation.
  • Reliable commitments — doing what you said you would do; not making promises you have no intention of keeping; letting your word be your bond (Matt. 5:37).

“For we are members one of another” — the argument behind the command. Paul does not merely say “stop lying”; he gives a reason, and the reason is ecclesiological. We are members of one another — meli esmen allēlōn — limbs of the same body. This is not a metaphor Paul is reaching for to illustrate a point; it is the reality he has been unfolding since 1:22. The church is Christ’s body, and every believer is a member of that body, joined to every other member as truly as a hand is joined to an arm.

The argument runs like this: Lying to a fellow member of the body is as irrational and destructive as one part of a body deceiving another. Imagine the eye sending false signals to the hand, or the nerve endings reporting no pain when the body is being damaged. The whole organism depends on accurate, truthful communication between its parts to function, to respond rightly, to survive. Falsehood within the body of Christ is not merely a personal moral failure; it is an attack on the body’s capacity to function. It erodes the trust that holds the community together. It causes the body to make decisions based on false information. It isolates members from one another behind carefully managed presentations. It prevents the mutual ministry of verse 12 from happening at all, because ministry requires knowing the real situation.

Conversely, the same argument is the most powerful positive motivation for truth-telling. You speak truthfully to your brother or sister not only because lying is wrong, but because they are yours — part of the same body, bound to you in Christ, dependent on you as you are on them. Truth is the oxygen of the body. Where it flows freely, the body is healthy, trust grows, and the kind of deep community Paul envisions in this letter becomes possible. Where it is replaced by management and performance, the body slowly suffocates. cf. Zech. 8:16; Rom. 12:5; 1 Cor. 12:26–27.

verseByVerse.quote: Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul quotes Psalm 4:4, acknowledging that anger is not always sin. Righteous anger at injustice and wickedness is appropriate. But unresolved anger becomes a foothold (topos — a position, a beachhead) for the devil. The warning is practical and urgent: deal with anger before nightfall. Resentment nursed overnight becomes bitterness; bitterness becomes a stronghold.

“And give no opportunity to the devil” (v. 27) — this is the verse the congregation most needs to hear alongside the permission to be angry. Topos means a place, a space, a foothold — the image is military: a beachhead from which an enemy can operate. Paul is saying that unresolved anger is not merely a personal problem or a relational inconvenience; it is a strategic opening. The devil does not need to break through your defences if you will hand him a position inside them.

Notice the logic of the passage. Verse 25 commands truth-telling because we are members of one body. Verse 26 allows anger but refuses to let it remain overnight. Verse 27 reveals why: the stakes are not merely emotional or relational — they are spiritual warfare. Every command in this section (vv. 25–32) is a command about how the body functions; every failure is an opportunity for the enemy to exploit. The devil’s strategy against the church is rarely frontal assault; it is the patient cultivation of small, unresolved grievances into entrenched divisions. A congregation where people nurse anger behind polite surfaces is a congregation giving the enemy exactly the foothold he needs.

What does “giving opportunity to the devil” look like in practice?

  • Rehearsing the offence. Replaying what was said or done, adding detail and weight with each retelling in the mind, until a small wound becomes a defining grievance. Every rehearsal deepens the foothold.
  • Telling others before telling the person. Sharing the grievance with a third party — framed as a prayer request, as concern, as seeking advice — rather than going directly to the one who offended (cf. Matt. 18:15). This plants the seed of faction.
  • Withholding forgiveness as power. Keeping the offence alive because it gives a sense of moral high ground or leverage in the relationship. This is the anger that has curdled into control.
  • Allowing distance to calcify. The sun goes down, then another, then a week, then a month. What could have been resolved by a five-minute honest conversation becomes a cold war that everyone around can feel but no one names. The body stops functioning at that joint.

The gospel answer is not the suppression of anger — “be angry” is a permission, not a rebuke — but its swift, honest resolution. The person who has been genuinely wronged is not required to pretend the wrong did not happen. They are required not to let it become a residence. Forgiveness is not a feeling; it is a decision to release the debt, made possible not by the worthiness of the offender but by the inexhaustible forgiveness already received in Christ (v. 32). The cross is the only place where the anger is rightly handled — laid down, not suppressed; absorbed, not avenged.

PREACHER’S NOTE The devil does not need to create new temptations if he can weaponise legitimate anger. Righteous indignation becomes pride; grief becomes self-pity; frustration becomes contempt. And crucially: the devil works slowly. He is content to wait while the sun goes down again and again. The gospel answer is not suppression but swift resolution — before the foothold becomes a fortress.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him labour, doing honest work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need.
verseByVerse.commentary: The logic is remarkable: the reason to stop stealing is not self-discipline but generosity. Work is not just economic survival but the means of having something to give. The gospel transforms the orientation of labour from acquisition to gift. Begg notes this is one of the most quietly radical ethical statements in the New Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sapros — rotten, putrid, the word for decaying food. Speech that tears down, gossips, belittles, or poisons the community is as out of place in the body of Christ as rotting meat at a feast. The positive standard is equally demanding: every word should be “good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear.”

A practical example. Two members of a small group have just heard that a third member, James, has lost his job. The first response: “Did you hear about James? I always thought he wasn’t really cut out for that role — apparently his boss had been frustrated with him for months.” That is sapros — speech that may be factually grounded but tears down, damages reputation, and poisons the way others will receive James when they next see him. It gives the hearers something that does not build them up and leaves James worse off in the community than before the words were spoken.

The second response: “James has just lost his job — he’s really shaken. Could we pray for him right now, and would one of us reach out this week?” Same information. Completely different direction. That word “fits the occasion,” gives grace to those who hear it, and moves the body toward the person in need rather than away from him. This is what Paul means. The question before every word is not “is this true?” but “does this build up? Does this give grace? Is this what this moment needs?” cf. Prov. 15:23: “a word in season — how good it is!”

verseByVerse.quote: And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This verse arrives like a sudden change of key — and it is meant to. Paul has been speaking about words and community, about the practical texture of life together. And then, without warning, he pulls back the curtain and shows us who is present in the room: the Holy Spirit of God himself, listening to every word, affected by every choice. This is not abstract theology; it is the most personal possible motivation for everything Paul has commanded.

What does it mean to grieve the Holy Spirit? The Greek is lypeō — to cause grief, to pain, to sadden. This is the word used of deep personal sorrow, the kind felt in close relationships. Paul is not saying the Spirit becomes angry, or that he withdraws his presence, or that the believer loses their salvation. He is saying something more intimate and more searching: the Spirit can be hurt. He is a Person — the third Person of the Trinity — not an impersonal force or a spiritual energy field. He has the full personal attributes of God, including the capacity for relational grief when love is spurned or holiness is violated by those he indwells.

How does grieving the Spirit happen? The context supplies the answer directly. Every command in verses 25–32 describes a way the Spirit can be grieved:

  • Falsehood (v. 25) — the Spirit is the “Spirit of truth” (John 16:13). Every lie spoken among believers grieves the one who is truth’s own advocate.
  • Unresolved anger (vv. 26–27) — the Spirit is the bond of peace (Eph. 4:3). Nursing resentment and giving the devil a foothold grieves the one who labours to unite what sin divides.
  • Corrupting speech (v. 29) — the Spirit works to build up the body. Every word that tears down works against him. He hears every conversation in every small group, every comment after the service, every message sent in frustration.
  • Bitterness, wrath, slander, malice (v. 31) — the Spirit produces love, joy, peace, patience, kindness (Gal. 5:22–23). These vices are the direct opposite of his fruit, and their presence in the community grieves him deeply.

More broadly, the Spirit is grieved whenever a believer treats sin casually, lives as though the old self were still in charge, or refuses the renewal he is working to bring about (vv. 22–24). He is not grieved by weakness, failure, or honest struggle — these he meets with intercession (Rom. 8:26). He is grieved by wilful, unrepentant persistence in what Christ died to remove.

“By whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” — what does this mean? The seal (sphragis) in the ancient world was the mark of ownership and the guarantee of authenticity — pressed into wax on a document or a jar, it said: this belongs to someone, and that someone stands behind it. Paul has already used this image in Ephesians 1:13–14: “you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it.” The Spirit himself is the seal. His presence in the believer is God’s own mark of ownership, God’s guarantee that what he has begun he will complete.

“The day of redemption” is the day of final deliverance — the return of Christ, the resurrection of the body, the full consummation of all that salvation means. The believer is not yet fully redeemed in experience; the body still groans, sin still remains, the world is still broken. But the seal is already applied. The Spirit’s presence now is the down payment (arrabōn, 1:14 — the first instalment that guarantees the rest) on a redemption that is as certain as God himself.

The argument embedded in “by whom you were sealed” is therefore both a warning and a wonder. The warning: do not grieve the very Person who is your guarantee of glory — who holds your future, who intercedes for you, who applies Christ’s work to your soul day by day. The wonder: the Spirit has not abandoned you despite your griefs. He grieves — and stays. He is sealed to you as surely as you are sealed by him. His grief is the grief of love that will not let go.

cf. Eph. 1:13–14; Isa. 63:10 (“they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit”); Rom. 8:23, 26–27; 2 Cor. 1:22; 1 Thess. 5:19 (“do not quench the Spirit”).

verseByVerse.quote: Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamour and slander be put away from you, along with all malice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six words. Paul lines them up like a row of weapons to be laid down — and each one is distinct. Together they describe the full arsenal of a heart that has refused the grace of verse 32. Understanding each term helps the reader see not just the category but the specific thing God is calling them to surrender.

Bitterness (pikria) — the deep, settled sourness of a soul that has been wounded and has chosen to nurse the wound rather than release it. Bitterness is what anger becomes when it is kept too long. It colours everything: the bitter person reads every new situation through the lens of old pain; they assume the worst, interpret generously toward no one, and carry a weight that poisons not only themselves but everyone around them. Hebrews 12:15 warns of a “root of bitterness” that springs up and “defiles many” — it is never merely personal. Bitterness is always communal in its damage.

Wrath (thymos) — the sudden flare, the hot explosion of passionate anger that erupts and then subsides. Unlike bitterness which is slow and cold, thymos is fast and hot — the flash of temper, the sharp word spoken in a moment of fury, the outburst that leaves wreckage behind.
