It is the anger that does not think before it speaks. James 1:19–20 addresses it directly: “be slow to anger, for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God.”

Anger (orgē) — where thymos is the sudden flare, orgē is the settled, brooding resentment that endures over time. It is the cold version of wrath — deliberate, sustained, often hidden. A person can appear perfectly calm while carrying orgē for years. It is the anger that builds a case, remembers every offence, and waits. Paul has already addressed this in verse 26: do not let the sun go down on it.

Clamour (kraugē) — the loud, public expression of anger: shouting, quarrelling, the raised voice that turns a disagreement into a scene. It is anger that has gone public and lost restraint. In the context of the community Paul is describing, clamour is the moment when a private grievance becomes a public fracture — the argument in the meeting, the confrontation after the service, the email written and sent in heat.

Slander (blasphēmia) — injurious speech about another person: damaging their reputation, speaking evil of them to others, whether the words are true or false. It includes gossip that is factually accurate but maliciously shared, and accusation that goes beyond what is warranted. In its root sense it is the same word used of blasphemy against God — it is speech that defiles and dishonours. Slander within the church is a particularly grievous form because it attacks the members of Christ’s body and therefore, in a real sense, Christ himself (cf. Acts 9:4).

Malice (kakia) — the underlying disposition from which all the others flow: a settled ill-will toward another person, a desire for their harm. It is the soil in which bitterness, wrath, anger, and slander all grow. Paul places it last because it is the root: a person with malice in their heart will find expression for it through all the other vices on the list. The call to put away malice is therefore the most fundamental of the six — it is the call to have the heart itself transformed, not merely the behaviour managed. cf. 1 Pet. 2:1; Col. 3:8.

verseByVerse.quote: Be kind to one another, tender-hearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having stripped the wardrobe bare in verse 31, Paul now furnishes it. Three words — kind, tender-hearted, forgiving — and then the ground on which all three stand: as God in Christ forgave you. This is not a command followed by a standard; it is a command that finds both its power and its pattern in what God has already done.

Kind (chrēstos) — practical, active goodness toward others; a readiness to serve, to meet a need, to go out of one’s way for another person’s benefit. It is the opposite of indifference. The word was used of wine that had mellowed with age — no longer sharp or harsh, but smooth and good. Jesus uses the same root in Matthew 11:30: “my yoke is chrēstos” — easy, gentle, well-fitting. Kindness in Paul’s sense is not merely pleasantness; it is the active disposition that looks for ways to be useful and good to the people around you, especially the difficult ones.

Tender-hearted (eusplagchnos) — literally “good-bowelled” in Greek, the bowels being in ancient thought the seat of deep emotion. It means a heart that is genuinely moved by another person’s pain — not hardened, not professionally sympathetic, but inwardly affected. The tender-hearted person does not manage other people’s suffering from a safe emotional distance; they feel it. This is the compassion of Christ himself, who was repeatedly described as being “moved with compassion” (splagchnizomai, the same root) when he encountered human need (Matt. 9:36; 14:14; Luke 15:20). The opposite of tender-heartedness is the hardness of heart Paul described in verse 18 — the calloused heart that has stopped feeling. The new self, created in God’s likeness, recovers the capacity to be moved.

Forgiving (charizomenoi) — this is the word that carries the full theological weight of the verse. It shares its root with charis — grace. To forgive in Paul’s sense is literally to grace someone: to give them what they do not deserve and cannot earn. It is not the same as excusing (pretending the wrong did not happen), nor is it the same as reconciliation (which requires repentance from the offender and may take time). Forgiveness is a unilateral decision of the will, made by the one who was wronged, to release the debt — to stop holding the offence as a claim, to refuse to let it define the relationship or fuel resentment.

Why is this so hard? Because forgiveness feels like injustice. It feels like letting the other person off the hook, like swallowing a wrong that deserves to be answered. This is why Paul grounds it entirely in the gospel: as God in Christ forgave you. The answer to the injustice objection is the cross. At the cross, the debt was not cancelled by pretending it did not exist; it was absorbed by the one who was wronged. God did not overlook sin; he paid for it himself, in Christ. Christian forgiveness follows the same pattern: you absorb the cost rather than pass it on. You take the loss rather than demand repayment. This is not weakness; it is the most costly and Christlike act a human being can perform. cf. Matt. 18:21–35; Col. 3:13; Luke 23:34.

God as the standard for all three — “as God in Christ forgave you” does not only ground the command to forgive; it sets the standard for all three virtues. God is kind: Romans 2:4 speaks of “the riches of his kindness.” God is tender-hearted: Psalm 103:13 — “as a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion.” God forgives: at infinite cost, freely, fully, finally. The Christian is not being asked to find these resources in themselves; they are being asked to pass on what they have already received. The measure of our giving is the measure of what we have been given — and what we have been given is immeasurable.

A practical example. Sarah and a colleague at church, Mark, had a falling out six months ago over a decision made in the worship team. Mark handled it badly — he was dismissive, spoke sharply in front of others, and never apologised. Sarah has been cold toward him since; she serves alongside him on Sunday mornings but keeps her distance, responds to his messages with minimum courtesy, and has told two friends what happened. She tells herself she has forgiven him because she no longer thinks about it every day.

Paul’s three words expose where she actually is. The kindness is gone — she has stopped looking for ways to serve or encourage Mark. The tender-heartedness has closed down — she does not want to know how he is doing. And the forgiveness is incomplete: she has released the acute pain but retained the verdict. The coolness, the strategic distance, the quiet word to two friends — these are the residue of an unforgiven debt still being held.

The way forward is not a feeling but a decision — made in prayer, grounded in the cross: Lord, I release this. Mark owes me nothing. I received forgiveness I did not deserve; I extend the same. Then the behaviour follows the decision: a genuine word toward Mark, an end to the quiet commentary to friends, a willingness to be present rather than managed. It will not feel natural immediately. It may need to be made again tomorrow. But this is what it looks like to live verse 32 in a real community, in a real week, with a real person who hurt you and never said sorry.

5.title: Walking in Love and the Mystery of Marriage
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children. <sup>2</sup>And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God. <sup>3</sup>But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints. <sup>4</sup>Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving. <sup>5</sup>For you may be sure of this, that everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous (that is, an idolater), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. <sup>6</sup>Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience. <sup>7</sup>Therefore do not become partners with them; <sup>8</sup>for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light <sup>9</sup>(for the fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true), <sup>10</sup>and try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord. <sup>11</sup>Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. <sup>12</sup>For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret. <sup>13</sup>But when anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible, <sup>14</sup>for anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” <sup>15</sup>Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, <sup>16</sup>making the best use of the time, because the days are evil. <sup>17</sup>Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is. <sup>18</sup>And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit, <sup>19</sup>addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, <sup>20</sup>giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, <sup>21</sup>submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ. <sup>22</sup>Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord. <sup>23</sup>For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. <sup>24</sup>Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands. <sup>25</sup>Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, <sup>26</sup>that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, <sup>27</sup>so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish. <sup>28</sup>In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. <sup>29</sup>For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church, <sup>30</sup>because we are members of his body. <sup>31</sup>“Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.” <sup>32</sup>This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church. <sup>33</sup>However, let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children." The command is breathtaking in its scope, and its motivation is everything. We are not to imitate God because He is powerful (though He is), or because He is sovereign (though He is), or even because He is just. We are to imitate God because we are His beloved children — because we have experienced the love of the Father, poured out in the gift of the Son, and children naturally, joyfully, instinctively imitate those who love them. The motivation for holy living is not duty but delight, not fear but love, not the dread of punishment but the joy of resemblance — looking like the Father who has claimed you as His own.

And the specific divine attribute to be imitated is love — but not love in the abstract. Paul immediately defines it: "as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God" (v.2). The love to be imitated is cruciform. It is the love that empties itself, that descends, that gives without counting the cost, that absorbs the worst and keeps on giving. The cross is not only the ground of our forgiveness; it is the template for our lives. Walk in love — the love that looks like Calvary.

Against this backdrop of self-giving love, the sexual immorality, impurity, and covetousness that Paul names in vv.3–5 are exposed as fundamentally loveless. They are forms of taking, not giving. They treat other persons and created things as objects for self-gratification rather than as gifts from God and neighbours to be loved. This is why Paul says they are not even to be named among God's holy people (v.3) — not because they are unspeakable, but because they are so alien to the character of those who have been loved with cruciform love that they simply don't belong. The gospel displaces them not primarily by prohibition but by offering something infinitely better: the love that transforms everything it touches.
verseByVerse.theology:
Cruciform Love as the Pattern of the Christian Life

"A fragrant offering and sacrifice to God" (v.2) — Paul's description of Christ's self-giving at the cross is drawn directly from the Old Testament sacrificial language. The burnt offering was described as "a pleasing aroma to the LORD" (Leviticus 1:9; 8:21) — a sacrifice that God receives with satisfaction, that expresses the proper worship of creature before Creator. Paul applies this language to the cross: the death of Christ was the ultimate sacrifice, the perfect offering, the worship that satisfied the holiness of God and secured the salvation of His people.

The implication for ethics is profound: to walk in love in imitation of Christ is to participate in a form of worship. Every act of genuine, self-giving love — every moment of costly service, every forgiveness extended at personal cost, every preference of another's need over one's own comfort — is offered to God as a fragrant offering. The Christian life is not divided into sacred acts (prayer, church attendance) and secular acts (daily life, work, relationships). All of it is worship. The love that looks like Calvary, lived out in the ordinary texture of daily life, is received by God as the aroma of Christ Himself.

Covetousness is identified in v.5 as idolatry — a striking identification that requires reflection. Covetousness is not merely wanting what others have; it is the orientation of the heart toward things rather than toward God, treating the creature as the source of satisfaction rather than the Creator. In this sense it is the root of sexual immorality as well: the sexualised culture is a culture of covetousness, of insatiable appetite, of treating persons as objects to be consumed. The gospel addresses this at the root by offering the only love that actually satisfies — the love of God in Christ, which surpasses knowledge and fills the fullness of God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: "Be imitators of God" — in the Greco-Roman world, this language had a specific resonance. The mystery religions and philosophical schools both spoke of homoiōsis theō — likeness to God — as the goal of the spiritual life. But the path they offered was typically ascetic withdrawal, esoteric knowledge, ritual elevation. Paul offers a radically different path: imitate the God who descended, who gave Himself up, who went to the cross for His enemies. The divine pattern to be imitated is not the god on the Olympian heights, remote and powerful, but the God who came down in love and poured Himself out in death. The imitation called for is not upward escape but downward love.

Now: Sexual immorality has been rebranded in our age as liberation, as authentic self-expression, as the natural pursuit of desire. Covetousness is marketed as aspiration, ambition, the engine of economic progress. Paul's gospel cuts through all of it — not with a longer list of prohibitions, but with a higher vision. You are a beloved child of the God who gave His Son for you. You have been loved with a love that went to the cross. Now walk in that love: freely, lavishly, cruciformly, without counting the cost. This is not the moralism of a killjoy god; it is the invitation of a Father who wants His children to look like Him and to know the joy of doing so.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children. And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mimētai tou theou — imitators of God. The Greek word gives us “mime.” A child mimics a parent in play; but the grown child imitates a father in earnest. The ground is “beloved children” — agapēta tekna. Our imitation of God flows from our adoption by God. The motivation is love received, not performance demanded.

The standard of love is the cross: Christ loved us and gave himself up, a fragrant offering to God. The cross is both the demonstration of love and the standard of love. Sproul: “The Christian ethic is not a list of rules but a love patterned on a sacrifice.” (cf. John 13:34; 1 John 3:16)

“A fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” — what did Paul mean? Paul is drawing on the deep language of the Old Testament sacrificial system, and every Jewish reader and God-fearer in Ephesus would have felt the weight of it immediately. In the Levitical sacrifices, a “fragrant offering” (reah nichoach in Hebrew, osmēn euōdias in Greek) was the phrase used when God declared himself pleased with what was offered — when the sacrifice was accepted, when the worshipper was received. It appears at the very first sacrifice after the flood (Gen. 8:21: “the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma”), throughout Leviticus for the burnt offerings and peace offerings (Lev. 1:9, 13, 17; 2:2; 3:5), and in Numbers for the daily offerings at the tabernacle. It is the language of divine acceptance — the sacrifice has reached God, God is pleased, the relationship is right.

Paul applies this entire weight to the cross. Christ’s self-giving is the ultimate sacrifice that all the Levitical offerings were pointing toward — the real thing that the animals could only foreshadow. Where every animal sacrifice required repetition because none was finally sufficient (Heb. 10:1–4), Christ’s offering was the one, final, fully accepted sacrifice: “a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Heb. 10:14). The fragrance that rose from every altar in Israel was always, in the purposes of God, anticipating this one moment — the Son of God giving himself, the Father accepting the offering, the broken relationship between God and humanity finally and fully restored.

Two words make the picture even richer:

  • Offering (prosphora) — a gift presented to God, something brought and laid before him. It stresses the voluntary nature of the act. Christ was not seized; he gave himself. John 10:18: “no one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord.” The love of verse 2 is precisely this: a free, voluntary self-giving for the benefit of others at infinite personal cost.
  • Sacrifice (thysia) — the actual act of slaughter, the costly giving up of life. Where prosphora stresses the giving, thysia stresses the cost. Together they hold the full reality of the cross: freely given (prosphora) and enormously costly (thysia). Neither the voluntariness nor the pain can be separated from the other.

And the result? God smells the fragrance and is satisfied. The wrath is propitiated (Rom. 3:25; 1 John 2:2). The broken covenant is restored. The guilty are declared righteous. What centuries of animal blood could only symbolise, the cross accomplished once and for all. This is the love Paul holds up as the standard and pattern for how believers are to love one another. Not romantic feeling, not natural affection, but cross-shaped, self-giving, costly love that asks not “what do I get?” but “what does this person need, and what will it cost me to give it?” cf. Heb. 9:14; 10:1–14; Rom. 3:25; 2 Cor. 2:14–15 (where the same fragrance language is applied to the spread of the gospel).

verseByVerse.quote: But sexual immorality and all impurity or covetousness must not even be named among you, as is proper among saints.
verseByVerse.commentary: Three vices — sexual immorality (porneia), impurity (akatharsia), covetousness (pleonexia) — are not merely to be avoided but not even named, not entering the vocabulary or the imagination of the community. “As is proper among saints” — the standard is identity, not merely morality. Saints are holy people, set apart; what defiles has no place in the set-apart community. Paul will name covetousness as idolatry in v. 5: the craving for more — whether sexual pleasure or material possession — is ultimately the worship of a false god placed in the seat that belongs to the Creator alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary: The catalog moves from deeds to words: filthiness (aischrotes), foolish talk (mōrologia), crude joking (eutrapelia). The Greco-Roman world celebrated wit and bawdy humor; Paul marks it as “out of place” (ou anekei) in the community of the cross. The antidote is striking: not solemn silence but thanksgiving (eucharistia). Gratitude is the natural speech of those who know what they have been given. A heart full of genuine thanksgiving has no room for talk that degrades; it overflows with praise. The same word gives us “Eucharist” — the language of the Lord’s table reframes all Christian speech.

verseByVerse.quote: For you may be sure of this, that everyone who is sexually immoral or impure, or who is covetous (that is, an idolater), has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul reveals the theological root of his warnings: sexual immorality and covetousness are not merely social failures — they are idolatry, and idolaters have no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God (cf. Col 3:5). The equation is penetrating: covetousness places the created thing in the position that belongs to God alone. “Empty words” (v. 6) are the sophistries of those who minimize the stakes: “God is gracious; these things don’t really matter.” Paul calls them lies. These are the very things for which God’s wrath falls on the sons of disobedience — not arbitrary punishment but the settled, holy opposition of the righteous God to all that destroys his image-bearers.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not become partners with them;
verseByVerse.commentary: “Therefore” draws the conclusion from the gravity of vv. 5–6: because these works bring wrath, and because the community belongs to the kingdom of light (v. 8), a clear distinction must be maintained. “Do not become partners” (mē ginesthe symmetochoi) — do not enter fellowship or complicity in these works. This is not an instruction to social isolation from unbelievers but a refusal to participate in the practices that belong to the old age. The church cannot be the church and also share in the works of darkness without fundamental self-contradiction.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"For at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord." The sharpness of this contrast arrests us every time we read it. Not "you were in darkness" — you were darkness itself. Not "you are now in the light" — you are light. The transformation is total, ontological, irreversible. Something has changed at the deepest level of what you are, not merely where you are or what you do. And the imperative that follows — "walk as children of light" — is not a command to achieve something new but to express something already true. Be in your behaviour what you are in your nature. Let the outside match the inside.

Light bears fruit. The fruit of light is "in all goodness and righteousness and truth" (v.9) — three qualities that together describe the character of the God who is light (1 John 1:5). The child of light is not defined primarily by what they avoid but by what they produce: genuine moral goodness, the rightness of life aligned with God's law and character, the transparency of truth-telling in every dimension of life. This fruit is not manufactured by effort; it grows naturally from a nature that has been fundamentally changed. Light cannot help but produce light-fruits.

And light exposes what darkness conceals. The children of light do not retreat from the darkness of the culture (withdrawal) or blend into it (accommodation). They expose it — by the simple, consistent, visible presence of a life lived in the open before God. This exposure is not aggressive or confrontational; it does not require denunciation or political engagement (though these may have their place). It requires holiness. "When anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible" (v.13). The most prophetic thing the church can do in a dark age is simply to be genuinely, visibly, persistently light.
verseByVerse.theology:
Light, Darkness, and the Prophetic Witness of Holiness

The ontological language of this passage — "you were darkness," "you are light" — reflects the radical nature of regeneration. The new birth is not a moral improvement programme; it is a change of nature. What was dark has become light. What was oriented toward self and sin has been reoriented toward God and holiness. This is the consistent teaching of the Reformed tradition: regeneration is sovereign, total, and irreversible — a work of God in the interior of the person that creates a new appetite, a new orientation, a new capacity for the things of God.

The call to "take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them" (v.11) raises the question of the church's relationship to culture. The Reformed tradition has generally resisted both the temptation to total withdrawal (a pietism that disengages from the world) and the temptation to total accommodation (a liberalism that conforms to it). The middle path — engagement without assimilation, presence without compromise — is what it means to be light in the world. The church that is genuinely, visibly holy is not only doing something good for its own members; it is doing something necessary for the world, exposing by contrast what the world cannot see about itself.

The awakening hymn of v.14 — "Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you" — is widely thought to be an early Christian baptismal hymn. It captures the eschatological urgency of the whole passage: the world is asleep, the darkness is presenting itself as normal and comfortable, and the church is called to be the community of the awakened, the risen, the enlightened. Not by shouting but by shining.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The darkness Paul describes in v.12 — "the things they do in secret" — was not merely a moral category. Ephesus had a fully developed underground of occult practice, of ritual darkness, of things done in the night that could not bear the daylight. The mystery religions operated precisely in the realm of secrets, of hidden things, of initiation into darkness. The church's commitment to transparency — to lives that could be lived fully in the open before God — was itself a form of witness against the culture of secrecy. You have nothing to hide because you have nothing to fear. You live in the light because Christ has shone on you.

Now: "Awake, O sleeper" has the ring of an alarm clock going off in a dark room. The world is sleeping — comfortable in its darkness, unaware of its danger, presenting its way of life as simply the normal and natural way to live. The church is called to wake up and to be awake — to see the world as it really is in the light of God's word, to live accordingly, and thereby to be the kind of community whose quality of life is itself an invitation: come and see what happens when Christ shines on you. In a culture that is drowsy with distraction and numbed by comfort, the church's wakefulness is among its most urgent callings.

verseByVerse.quote: for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul does not say they were in darkness and are now in light. He says they were darkness and are light — a change of nature, not merely of location. This is the new birth in moral language: the very substance of what they are has been transformed by union with Christ, who is the light of the world (John 8:12). “Walk as children of light” — the indicative becomes the imperative. You do not walk in the light to become light; you walk as light because you already are light in the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: (for the fruit of light is found in all that is good and right and true), and try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary: The parenthesis defines what light naturally produces: goodness (agathōsynē — moral excellence), righteousness (dikaiosynē — right relation to others), and truth (alētheia — integrity, correspondence with reality). These three are not rules to perform but fruit to bear — the natural produce of a life transformed into light. Verse 10 adds the daily discipline: “try to discern what is pleasing to the Lord” (dokimazein — test, evaluate, approve after examination). The Spirit-filled life requires active moral discernment, constantly asking what honors Christ in this specific situation.

verseByVerse.quote: Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them. For it is shameful even to speak of the things that they do in secret.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Unfruitful works of darkness” — fruitlessness is the mark of the old life; where the fruit of light is good, right, and true, the works of darkness bear nothing that survives. The command is not only to abstain but to expose (elenchein — rebuke, convict, bring into the open). This does not require lurid description; v. 12 notes that what is done in secret is too shameful even to name. Exposure happens through contrast: the sheer presence of lives lived in light makes darkness visible without needing to enumerate its contents in detail.

verseByVerse.quote: But when anything is exposed by the light, it becomes visible, for anything that becomes visible is light. Therefore it says, 'Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The logic is arresting: when light exposes darkness, the exposed thing becomes light — transformed by the very exposure that reveals it. This describes both the conversion of sinners (their sin brought into the open by the gospel, they are transformed) and the purification of the community (sins dealt with openly are healed).

The hymn fragment of v. 14 — “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you” — is almost certainly a quotation, introduced by Paul’s “for it says” (dió legei), the same formula used to introduce OT Scripture (e.g., 4:8; 5:14). But the words do not appear verbatim anywhere in the OT. Preachers should explain the three possibilities: (1) An OT conflation: the words draw on Isaiah 26:19 (“Your dead shall live… awake and sing for joy”) and Isaiah 60:1 (“Arise, shine, for your light has come”) — Paul weaves the two resurrection-and-light passages together. (2) An early Christian baptismal hymn (the majority modern scholarly view — Lincoln, Fee, Thielman): this was a hymn fragment sung in the primitive church, possibly at baptisms, where the one being baptized was called to “arise” from the waters as from death, into the light of Christ. Paul cites it as authoritative early Christian confession. (3) A lost apocryphal source: the Father Epiphanius attributed these words to an “Apocalypse of Elijah”; modern scholars regard this as unlikely. The most defensible reading: Paul quotes a Spirit-inspired early church hymn that itself distills OT resurrection-and-light imagery, and applies it as an evangelistic call to the sleeper who has not yet risen into Christ’s light. The text is a call to conversion expressed through the language of resurrection — the same language Paul has been using for salvation throughout the letter (2:1–6).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil." The third walk imperative carries a quality of urgency that is eschatological in character. The Christian does not live in a neutral moment; they live in a moment freighted with significance, in days that are evil (and therefore time-limited in their evil), in a window of opportunity that will not remain open forever. Wisdom means seeing this clearly and acting accordingly — not frantic and anxious, but alert and intentional, making the most of every opportunity because the Kingdom has come and its King is returning.

The contrast Paul draws between drunkenness and fullness of the Spirit is one of the most theologically provocative contrasts in the letter. He is not simply contrasting vice and virtue, or bad behaviour and good. He is contrasting two kinds of fullness — two ways of trying to transcend the ordinary, to escape the limitations of sober consciousness, to find ecstasy. Wine offers dissolution — the loss of self, the blurring of edges, the temporary escape from sobriety into sensation. The Spirit offers something entirely different: not the loss of self but the fullness of self as God intended it, overflowing with a joy that is oriented outward, that expresses itself in song and gratitude and the mutual submission that makes genuine community possible.

The Spirit-filled life Paul describes is intensely communal in its expression. It erupts in singing — "psalms and hymns and spiritual songs" (v.19) — a rich triad suggesting the full range of musical and devotional expression available to the church. It issues in "giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ" — a gratitude so comprehensive that nothing is excluded from its scope. And it produces "submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ" — the mutual humility that Paul will apply to marriage, family, and household in the verses that follow. The Spirit-filled community looks and sounds different from the world around it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Fullness of the Spirit and the Worshipping Community

"Be filled with the Spirit" (v.18) is a present passive imperative — go on being filled, continuously, repeatedly. The fullness of the Spirit is not a one-time crisis experience; it is the ongoing reality of a life open to and dependent on God's Spirit. The passive voice is significant: we do not fill ourselves; we are filled. We create the conditions — prayer, the word, corporate worship, obedience — and God does the filling. Calvin wrote that the Spirit is given to those who ask (Luke 11:13), and that the asking must be persistent, humble, and expectant.

The triad of "psalms and hymns and spiritual songs" (v.19) has been the subject of considerable historical discussion about the nature of Christian worship. The Reformed tradition has generally understood the Psalms as the divinely given hymnal of the church, with "hymns and spiritual songs" expanding the range of legitimate worship expression. What matters more than the categorisation is the character: the worship is corporate, directed toward God, spirit-animated, joyful, and overflowing into the rest of life. Worship is not an event on Sunday that is unrelated to life on Monday; it is the expression of a fullness that shapes everything the Spirit-filled person does.

The closing imperative — "submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ" (v.21) — is the theological hinge on which everything that follows turns. Paul will apply mutual submission to wives and husbands, children and fathers, servants and masters. But the foundation is the mutual submission of the Spirit-filled community: a posture of other-centredness, of preferring one another, of deferring in love to the needs and preferences of those around us. This is the overflow of a life that has been filled with the Spirit of the One who "did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself" (Philippians 2:6–7).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The worship of Artemis and the mystery religions of Ephesus were soaked in wine, in ecstatic states, in the pursuit of transcendence through altered consciousness. The Dionysian festivals were characterized by drunkenness and sexual abandon as means of communing with the divine. Against this entire religious culture, Paul offers the Spirit-filled community as the true alternative: not the dissipation of Dionysus but the fullness of the Holy Spirit, not the frantic ecstasy of the cult but the joyful, ordered, outward-facing overflow of a community that has been possessed not by wine but by God. The church was, in Ephesus, a genuinely countercultural gathering — a community whose worship looked and sounded like nothing else in the city.

Now: We live in an age of spiritual hunger and an age of extraordinary means for filling the void — entertainment, substance, distraction, the endless dopamine of the digital feed. None of it satisfies. The hunger returns, more insistent than before. Paul's word to a hungry generation is unchanged: be filled with the Spirit. The fullness He gives is not the temporary satiation of appetite but the genuine, overflowing, outward-directed joy of a life in which God Himself has taken up residence. The church that is genuinely, visibly, joyfully full of the Spirit — that sings with gratitude, that submits in love, that gives thanks for everything — is offering the watching world a glimpse of what it was made for.

verseByVerse.quote: Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Look carefully” (blepete akribōs) — precise, deliberate attention to the direction of one’s life. The contrast is wise (sophos) versus unwise — wisdom being the God-given capacity to see life as God sees it and live accordingly. Exagorazomenoi ton kairon — “buying up the time” or redeeming the opportunity. Kairos is not clock time but the critical moment, the opportunity that may not come again. “The days are evil” — the present age is morally compromised, hostile to the things of God. Precisely because the environment is dangerous and the opportunities precious, the believer must move through time with costly intention.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Foolish” (aphrones — without moral understanding) is the opposite of the wisdom urged in vv. 15–16. The antidote is not more information but understanding (synientes — grasping with the mind and living from that grasp) of what the will of the Lord is. This is the great orienting question of the wise life: not what is convenient, what is acceptable, what everyone else is doing — but what does the Lord want here? This understanding comes through Scripture, Spirit, and the counsel of the community, and it becomes the steering mechanism of the redeemed life.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary: The contrast is not arbitrary. Wine was central to the ecstatic cults of Ephesus — intoxication as the path to spiritual experience, the self surrendered to an external power. Paul refuses the counterfeit: not wine (in which is asōtia — dissolution, the self without restraint) but the Spirit. “Be filled” (plērousthe) is present passive — ongoing, continually, by the Spirit’s action not your effort. You do not fill yourself; you position yourself to be filled. And what follows immediately (vv. 19–21) is entirely relational: Spirit-filling is not private mystical experience but community transformation. (cf. Acts 2:4; Col. 3:16)

verseByVerse.quote: addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary: The Spirit-filled life overflows in song and thanksgiving. Three types of song — psalms (the OT Psalter, the church’s permanent hymnbook), hymns (focused doxology), spiritual songs (Spirit-prompted expression) — fill the community’s common life. “Addressing one another” — worship is mutual and horizontal as well as vertical; believers build one another up in song. “Making melody to the Lord with your heart” — the music is not performance but from the heart. “Giving thanks always and for everything” (eucharistountes pantote hyper pantōn) — the scope is total: always, for everything, because God the Father is sovereign and Jesus Christ is the mediator of every blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: This verse is the hinge between the Spirit-filled life (vv. 18–20) and the household code (vv. 22–6:9). “Submitting to one another” (hypotassomenoi allēlois) — mutual submission is the atmosphere of the Spirit-filled community; each person placing the other above themselves. “Out of reverence for Christ” (en phobō Christou) makes Christ, not social convention, the motive for every submissive relationship. The household code that follows is not a baptism of Greco-Roman social structures but an application of this Christ-governed mutual submission to the concrete realities of household life.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
From the Spirit-filled community of mutual submission (v.21), Paul descends into the most intimate community of all — marriage — and what he finds there is not merely a domestic arrangement to be governed by wise principles but a living, breathing proclamation of the gospel itself. The move from v.21 to v.22 is seamless and deliberate: the mutual submission of the Spirit-filled community finds its most profound and most costly expression in the marriage covenant. And Paul's disclosure in v.32 — "this mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church" — reveals that marriage was never merely about human beings. It was always a sign pointing beyond itself to the most magnificent love story in the universe.

The husband is called to love his wife as Christ loved the church — and the standard is Calvary. He gave himself up. He poured himself out. He loved the undeserving, the faithless, the sinful, and He loved them to the uttermost. The husband who reads Ephesians 5:25 in earnest will never again use his headship as a platform for self-assertion or self-service. He will wield it with trembling, knowing that the pattern he is called to embody is the pattern of the cross. And the purpose of his love — that she might be sanctified, cleansed, presented without spot or wrinkle — reveals that the husband's calling is not merely to make his wife happy but to invest in her holiness, to be the kind of man whose love makes her more fully herself in Christ.

Paul's "profound mystery" (v.32) is the key to the entire passage. Marriage was designed from the beginning as a visible, embodied proclamation of the love between Christ and His church. Every faithful Christian marriage — every husband who loves with cruciform love, every wife who trusts and honours her husband — is enacting the gospel, displaying the love of Christ, bearing witness to the covenant that holds even when everything else fails. The watching world, the children, the neighbours, the colleagues — they see something in a genuinely Christ-shaped marriage that they cannot produce on their own: a love that holds, that forgives, that persists, that grows more beautiful with time. They are seeing the love of Christ in human form.

The household code tradition (Haustafeln): Preachers who have read Aristotle or studied Greco-Roman ethics will recognize that Paul is engaging with a well-established literary genre. Ancient moralists — Aristotle (Politics 1:1253b), the Stoic Hierocles, and later Hellenistic Jewish writers (Philo, Josephus) — regularly taught household management through three pairs of relationships: husband/wife, parent/child, master/slave. This genre is called Haustafeln (the German term, “household tablets,” introduced by Luther). Paul uses the same three-pair structure, which would have been immediately recognizable to any educated reader. But his version is radically and deliberately different in four ways: (1) He addresses the subordinate party first: wives, children, and slaves are addressed directly before husbands, fathers, and masters — in ancient household codes, only the dominant party was addressed. The subordinate parties were spoken about, not to. Paul’s direct address gives them full moral standing as agents accountable to Christ. (2) Every command is grounded in Christ: not in nature, not in social utility, not in philosophical reason — “as to the Lord,” “as Christ loved the church,” “in the Lord.” The entire code is Christologically transformed. (3) The dominant party receives the longer and more demanding command: husbands get nine verses (vv. 25–33); wives get three (vv. 22–24). The asymmetry is entirely against ancient custom. (4) The household is embedded in mutual submission (5:21): the code is introduced not by “husbands rule” but by “submit to one another out of reverence for Christ.” The form is conventional; the content is a quiet revolution.
verseByVerse.theology:
Marriage, Headship, and the Gospel Mystery

Ephesians 5:22–33 is the most theologically freighted passage on marriage in all of Scripture. Its central claim — that marriage is a living image of the relationship between Christ and the church — elevates the institution beyond any merely human social arrangement. Marriage is a sign. Its structure (the husband's headship, the wife's willing embrace of it) is not arbitrary or culturally conditioned; it images something real and eternal: the self-giving authority of Christ over His church, and the church's joyful, trusting response to her Lord.

The husband's headship is defined entirely by the cross: "as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her" (v.25). Any interpretation of headship that does not immediately move to sacrifice and self-giving has misread the passage. The head of the church is the one who died for it, who washed it, who nourishes and cherishes it (v.29). The husband who exercises headship in this mode is not dominating but descending — following the pattern of the One who "came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many" (Matthew 20:28).

The wife's calling — to "submit to your own husband, as to the Lord" (v.22) — is the free, willing, graced response of a woman who is secure in Christ. It is not coerced compliance; it is the image of the church's joyful response to her loving Lord. This mutual imaging of the gospel — husband as Christ, wife as church — requires both partners to draw from wells deeper than themselves. No man can love his wife as Christ loved the church from his own resources; no woman can embody the church's response to Christ on her own. Both require the same Spirit who filled the community in v.18. Marriage is a Spirit-dependent vocation for both.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In the Greco-Roman world, the husband's authority over his wife was nearly absolute and assumed to be primarily for his benefit. The paterfamilias was the household's lord in every sense. Paul's command for husbands to love their wives sacrificially — to give themselves up for them, to nourish and cherish them as their own bodies — was not a reinforcement of existing cultural norms. It was their radical subversion. The Roman husband used his authority to be served. The Christian husband was to use his authority to serve. This was not a minor adjustment to the household code; it was a revolution grounded in the cross.

Now: Christian marriage swims against two powerful currents simultaneously. The first is the culture's dismissal of permanent covenant — the reduction of marriage to an expressive partnership that may be dissolved when it no longer meets individual needs. The second is the sometimes shallow version of complementarianism that invokes headship without the cross, demanding submission without offering service. Against both, Ephesians 5 offers the third way: covenant love, shaped by the cross, sustained by the Spirit, oriented toward the other's flourishing, and pointing always beyond itself to the love that holds the universe together. A marriage like this is a miracle — and miracles point to a Miracle Worker.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary: The verb “submit” is not present in the Greek of v. 22 — it carries over from the mutual submission of v. 21 (hypotassomenoi). Wives are called to the same posture Paul has just called every believer to adopt toward one another, applied in the specific relation to their own husbands. “As to the Lord” — not because the husband is divine, but because the wife’s submission is ultimately an act of obedience to Christ who has ordered marriage this way. The husband’s authority is borrowed and bounded; the wife’s submission is given to God himself through this divinely appointed structure.

verseByVerse.quote: For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul grounds the husband’s headship in the analogy of Christ’s headship over the church — and this analogy both establishes and radically reshapes the authority it grants. Christ is head and Savior; he gave himself for the church, nourishes and cherishes it (v. 29). Headship is servant-leadership, cross-shaped from the start. “His body” — the church is not beneath Christ but united to him, inseparable. “In everything” does not mean blind obedience without limit — the analogy itself provides the limit: the church submits to Christ, not to anyone who contradicts him. No human husband may command what the Lord forbids.

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her,
verseByVerse.commentary: The husband receives the longer and more demanding instruction. His love is measured by the cross. The verb is agapaō — self-giving covenant love, not sentiment. “As Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” — this is the standard: the willingness to give oneself completely for the good of the beloved, at the cost of everything. Paul does not say “lead your wives” first; he says “love your wives.” The leadership is shaped entirely by the love; the authority exists to serve the beloved’s flourishing, not to assert itself. (cf. Col. 3:19; 1 Pet. 3:7)

verseByVerse.quote: that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish.
verseByVerse.commentary: The purpose of Christ’s self-giving is the church’s sanctification and final glorification. “The washing of water with the word” — the external sign of baptism and the proclaimed gospel work together. Christ’s purpose for his bride is holiness — progressive now, perfect at the last. “Present the church to himself in splendor” — the imagery of the radiant bride at the wedding, every blemish removed by his own atoning work. The husband who loves like Christ sets before himself not a program of control but a vision of his wife’s holiness and flourishing as the telos of his entire life with her. Stott: “No husband has loved his wife as Christ has loved the church; but this remains the standard toward which all Christian husbands strive.”

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul shifts from the Christological standard to the creational reality: in marriage, the two become one flesh (v. 31, citing Gen 2:24). Therefore to love the wife is to love what is, in a profound sense, oneself. This is not narcissism but the logic of union: the husband who nurtures and cares for his wife is tending the one-flesh reality that includes himself. The converse is equally true: the husband who neglects or wounds his wife injures himself. The union created in marriage is so real that what is done to one is done to both.

verseByVerse.quote: For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church, because we are members of his body.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Nourishes” (ektrephei) and “cherishes” (thalpei — literally, to warm) — the language of tender, careful provision. Paul’s point: self-care is natural and instinctive; no one destroys their own body. Marriage extends this instinct to the wife who is, in the mystery of one flesh, the husband’s own body. And the analogy returns to Christ: he nourishes and cherishes the church because “we are members of his body.” The church is not external to Christ but united to him in a union the cross created and the Spirit maintains. The husband’s tenderness toward his wife is thus patterned on the most patient and self-giving love in existence.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh. This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul cites Genesis 2:24 — the creation foundation of marriage — and then makes a breathtaking hermeneutical claim: the mystērion embedded in this text has always referred to Christ and the church. The leaving and cleaving, the one-flesh union — all of it has been a sign pointing beyond itself to the union of the incarnate Son with the humanity he came to save. This does not make marriage less real; it makes it more glorious. Every faithful marriage is a living icon of the gospel: the self-giving of Christ for his bride, the response of the church in love and trust. The mystery hidden in Genesis 2 has been disclosed in Ephesians 5. (cf. Gen. 2:24; Rev. 19:7–9)

verseByVerse.quote: However, let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary: The soaring theology resolves into immediate, personal application: each one, his wife, her husband — the singular weight of it. Love (agapaō) for the husband; respect (phobos — reverence, honor) for the wife. These are not identical but complementary. The husband’s deepest need is to be respected; the wife’s deepest need is to be loved. Paul addresses each at the point of their calling and their vulnerability. “As himself” — self-love is the measure; the husband who cares for his wife with the same attention he gives to his own wellbeing has understood what the one-flesh union requires of him.

6.title: Household Duties and the Armour of God
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. <sup>2</sup>“Honor your father and mother” (this is the first commandment with a promise), <sup>3</sup>“that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land.” <sup>4</sup>Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. <sup>5</sup>Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as you would Christ, <sup>6</sup>not by the way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but as bondservants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, <sup>7</sup>rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man, <sup>8</sup>knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether he is a bondservant or is free. <sup>9</sup>Masters, do the same to them, and stop threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him. <sup>10</sup>Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might. <sup>11</sup>Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil. <sup>12</sup>For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. <sup>13</sup>Therefore take up the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand firm. <sup>14</sup>Stand therefore, having fastened on the belt of truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, <sup>15</sup>and, as shoes for your feet, having put on the readiness given by the gospel of peace. <sup>16</sup>In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; <sup>17</sup>and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, <sup>18</sup>praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication. To that end, keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints, <sup>19</sup>and also for me, that words may be given to me in opening my mouth boldly to proclaim the mystery of the gospel, <sup>20</sup>for which I am an ambassador in chains, that I may declare it boldly, as I ought to speak. <sup>21</sup>So that you also may know how I am and what I am doing, Tychicus the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord will tell you everything. <sup>22</sup>I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are, and that he may encourage your hearts. <sup>23</sup>Peace be to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>24</sup>Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Spirit-filled community of 5:18–21, expressed in the marriage covenant of 5:22–33, now extends into the full household: children and parents, servants and masters. These are not grand or glamorous relationships — they are the daily, ordinary, sometimes tedious texture of domestic life. And yet Paul charges every one of them with gospel significance. The Spirit who fills the worshipping community also fills the kitchen, the nursery, the workshop, the field. There is no space in the Christian household that is exempt from the Lordship of Christ, no relationship that lies outside the sanctifying reach of the gospel.

The commands are given with careful balance. Children are told to obey — but fathers are immediately told not to provoke. Servants are told to serve faithfully — but masters are immediately told to treat their servants with justice and fairness. In every pair, both parties receive commands; in every pair, both parties are accountable to Christ. This symmetry is itself a theological statement: in the household of the Spirit-filled community, no one is merely the recipient of others' service and no one is merely the dispenser of commands. All are servants of Christ, all are accountable to the same Lord, all are engaged in the same vocation of making their ordinary relationships a theatre of God's glory.

The motivating principle that runs through the entire passage is Paul's repeated phrase "as to the Lord" or "as slaves of Christ." The child who obeys parents is obeying "in the Lord" (v.1). The servant who works faithfully does so "as to the Lord and not to men" (v.7). The master treats servants justly "knowing that he also has a Master in heaven" (v.9). Every human authority is relativised by a higher authority; every human service is dignified by being rendered to Christ. The gospel transforms every relationship in the household not by changing its external form but by changing the motivation, the orientation, and the significance of everything done within it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Authority, Service, and the Lordship of Christ

The household codes of Ephesians 5:22–6:9 have sometimes been misread as Paul's accommodation to Roman social structures — a domestication of the gospel that reinforces existing hierarchies. The opposite is true. Paul takes every relationship in the household and transforms it from within by the same double principle: both parties have obligations, and both parties are accountable to Christ. This is not the endorsement of hierarchy for its own sake; it is the sanctification of ordered relationships by the presence of a Lord who stands above every human ordering.

The instruction to servants (vv.5–8) is particularly searching. "Obey... as you would Christ," "doing the will of God from the heart," "rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man, knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord." Paul is not telling slaves that their situation is just; he is telling them that no situation, however unjust, is outside the reach of Christ's transforming presence. The servant who works faithfully for an unworthy master, doing it as for the Lord, is engaged in genuine worship — and will receive the Lord's commendation at the last day, whatever commendation or condemnation the human master gave or withheld.

The warning to masters — "do the same to them, and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him" (v.9) — is one of the most socially radical statements in the New Testament. The master has a Master. The one with authority is under authority. Before the throne of the impartial God, all distinctions of status dissolve. This truth, fully believed and consistently applied, has done more to dismantle unjust social structures than any legal or political programme. It was ultimately the logic of this verse, applied over centuries, that made slavery in the Christian world an untenable contradiction.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Roman paterfamilias held virtually absolute authority over his household — his wife, his children, and his slaves were all, in various degrees, subject to his legal control. Children had no independent legal standing; slaves were property. Paul's household code addresses children and slaves first, and addresses them as moral agents capable of genuine obedience to God — not as objects to be managed. This is itself a dignity-claim that the Roman household code did not make. And the commands to fathers (don't exasperate) and masters (treat them justly) placed obligations on the powerful toward the powerless that Roman law did not require. The Christian household was different — visibly, consistently, counter-culturally different.

Now: "Children, obey your parents in the Lord" and "Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger" — both imperatives are needed in every age, and our age tends to violate both simultaneously. We live in a culture that simultaneously refuses to discipline children (producing entitled, poorly-bounded young people) and fails to give them the patient, encouraging, Christ-centred nurture that Ephesians 6:4 envisions. The Christian home where authority is exercised in love, where children are both appropriately disciplined and genuinely encouraged in the Lord, where the name of Christ is spoken and the word of God is read — this home is a counterculture, a community of formation in a world that has largely forgotten what formation is for.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
verseByVerse.commentary: “In the Lord” qualifies and deepens the obedience: children obey not merely because parents have authority but because Christ is Lord of the household and has ordered it this way. “This is right” (dikaion estin) — not merely commanded but fitting, consistent with the created order and the moral structure of the family. Paul addresses children directly — they are full members of the congregation, present when the letter is read aloud, accountable to Christ for their own response to his word. The qualifier “in the Lord” also provides the limit: obedience is within the scope of the Lord’s own commands, not extending to what Christ himself forbids. (cf. Col. 3:20; Prov. 1:8)

verseByVerse.quote: Honor your father and mother (this is the first commandment with a promise), that it may go well with you and that you may live long in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul reaches to the fifth commandment (Exod 20:12; Deut 5:16) and notes its distinction: it carries a promise. “Honor” (timē) is broader than childhood obedience — it encompasses the ongoing respect, care, and esteem owed to parents through adult life. The promise of well-being and longevity reflects a wisdom God has built into human community: the generation that honors parents sustains the social fabric across time. Paul takes the OT promise seriously and applies it to the church. The commandment outlasts the household; it shapes the posture of the grown child toward aging parents long after direct obedience is no longer the primary mode of the relationship.

verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prohibition is precise: do not parorgizete — exasperate, embitter, provoke. The word carries the weight of constant, demoralising criticism, unreasonable demands, or the cold withdrawal of love. These break the spirit rather than shape it.

The positive command is threefold in its depth: ektrephete (nourish, bring to full growth), paideia (structured training and correction), nouthesia (verbal instruction, counsel, admonition) — and all of it kyriou, of the Lord. The father is not forming the child in the father’s image but in the Lord’s image. The whole household is under Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as you would Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul addresses the slave first — itself a gesture of moral dignity in a world where slaves were often treated as property without standing. The command is for whole-hearted service: “fear and trembling” is not terror but the solemn awareness of standing before the living God. “With a sincere heart” (en haplotēti tēs kardias) — singleness of heart, without duplicity. “As you would Christ” — the real master is not the human employer but the Lord who observes all and to whom account is given. This fundamentally relativizes every human authority without removing the obligation of faithful service.

verseByVerse.quote: not by the way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but as bondservants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, rendering service with a good will as to the Lord and not to man,
verseByVerse.commentary: “Eye-service” (ophthalmodoulia) — Paul coins a word: working only when watched, performing only for the observing eye. This is the default mode of coerced labor. The alternative is not better performance management but a different master: “bondservants of Christ.” When the ultimate audience is Christ — who sees all, records all, and will reward all — the human supervisor’s presence or absence becomes irrelevant. “From the heart” and “with a good will” — the quality of the work changes entirely when the audience changes. Labor offered to the Lord is worship; labor performed for human approval is performance.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether he is a bondservant or is free.
verseByVerse.commentary: The great equalizer: divine justice makes no distinction of social status. “Whether he is a bondservant or is free” — the slave and the freeman stand before the same judge and receive the same reward for faithful labor. No deed done for the Lord is wasted, overlooked, or unrewarded, whether it was performed in a position of prestige or in a slave quarter. Calvin: “God is no respecter of persons; the service of the most humbled slave, done in faith, is as acceptable to him as the offering of kings.” This is a profound subversion of every social hierarchy: the eternal calculus does not follow the ledgers of Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: Masters, do the same to them, and stop threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The master is brought under the same rubric as the slave. He has a Master. His authority is delegated and conditional. He is to treat his slaves with the same integrity of heart he expects from them — “do the same.” The specific prohibition — stop threatening — targets the master’s most characteristic abuse of power. The reason is theological: God shows no partiality. Social status confers no advantage before the throne of heaven.

This was not an anti-slavery manifesto in the modern sense; it was something more radical in the long run — it placed master and slave under the same moral governance, the same eternal accountability, the same Lord. The logic, followed to its conclusion, is incompatible with slavery as an institution.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The letter's great climax — and it arrives without warning, like a general stepping out of his tent to address his troops before the decisive battle. "Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might." Everything that has preceded — the cosmic vision of God's purposes, the theology of grace, the ethics of the Spirit-filled community, the transformed household — now finds its context: the Christian life is warfare. Not metaphorical warfare, not a polite spiritual competition, but genuine, cosmic, personal, urgent conflict with "the rulers, the authorities, the cosmic powers over this present darkness, the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places" (v.12).

The armour Paul describes is not human equipment; it is divine provision. Each piece is identified with a theological reality rather than a military material. The belt is truth. The breastplate is righteousness. The boots are readiness given by the gospel of peace. The shield is faith. The helmet is salvation. The sword is the word of God. Roman soldiers would have recognized every item in this list; Paul is taking the most powerful military image of his world and filling it entirely with theological content, because the battle that matters is not on the human plane and cannot be won with human weapons.

The repeated command is to stand — four times in seven verses (vv.11, 13, 14). Not to advance on our own initiative, not to conquer by our own strength, but to hold the ground that Christ has already secured against a defeated enemy who refuses to concede. The Christian stands in the victory of the resurrection, armed with the provisions of the ascended Lord, and sustained — above all things — by prayer. "Praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication" (v.18) — the armour is not self-sustaining; it functions within an ongoing relationship with the Commander, through whose power alone the standing is possible.
verseByVerse.theology:
Spiritual Warfare and the Victory of Christ

The passage grounds the doctrine of spiritual warfare in the victory already achieved by Christ. The Reformers consistently insisted that the Christian fights from victory, not toward it. At the cross and resurrection, Christ decisively defeated the powers: "He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him" (Colossians 2:15). The "rulers and authorities" of Ephesians 6:12 are already defeated enemies — real, malevolent, and active, but operating under the authority of One who has conquered them. The Christian's warfare is not the decisive battle; it is the mopping-up operation conducted in light of a victory already won.

This context — victory already achieved — is what makes "standing" the characteristic posture of the Christian warrior rather than "advancing." Paul does not say "take more territory." He says "stand." Hold what Christ has secured. Don't give ground to a defeated enemy. Don't abandon the position that grace has placed you in. This is not a passive posture; it requires every piece of armour, every act of faith, every prayer offered in the Spirit. But it is a posture of confidence, not of uncertainty — the confidence of those who know how the battle ends and who are fighting in the strength of its Victor.

Prayer (vv.18–20) is the atmosphere in which the armoured Christian stands. It is "at all times in the Spirit" — not occasional, not formal, but the constant, Spirit-sustained reaching toward the Commander. Paul's request for prayer for himself (vv.19–20) is among the most searching things in the letter. The apostle who has written the most magnificent theological letter in the New Testament asks his readers to pray that he would have the boldness to speak the gospel clearly. He is acutely aware that the proclamation of the gospel is itself a spiritual warfare activity, requiring not merely intellectual preparation but Spirit-given courage and divine enablement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ephesus was a city saturated with occult practice. The book of Acts records that when the gospel came to Ephesus, it confronted demonic powers directly — the sons of Sceva, the burning of the magic books, the riot engineered by Demetrius the silversmith whose trade in Artemis-shrines was threatened (Acts 19). The Ephesian Christians knew, from personal experience, that spiritual warfare was real. When Paul tells them to stand against "the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places," he is not speaking metaphorically to a congregation that has only ever faced theoretical opposition. He is arming people who have already been in the fight.

Now: The tendency in contemporary Christianity is to spiritualise spiritual warfare into invisibility (it's just a metaphor for human sin and social structures) or to sensationalise it into obsession (seeing demonic activity behind every difficulty). Paul's teaching steers between both errors. The powers are real — personal, intelligent, malevolent. But they are defeated — operating under the authority of the risen Christ who has already triumphed over them. The Christian response is neither to ignore them nor to be paralyzed by them, but to stand — in the truth, in righteousness, in the gospel, in faith, in salvation, in the word of God, and in unceasing prayer. This is neither the naivety of the denier nor the anxiety of the obsessed. It is the steady, armoured confidence of those who know their Commander.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Finally” marks the climactic practical section of the letter. The exhortation to strength is passive: endunamousthe — be empowered, receive strength from without. The source is “the Lord” — the exalted Christ who has already defeated every enemy (1:20–22). “The strength of his might” (kratous tēs ischyos autou) — three terms for power, the same language used in 1:19 for the power that raised Christ from the dead. The battle Paul is about to describe is not fought in the believer’s own resources but in the inexhaustible power of the one who has already won.

verseByVerse.quote: Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil. For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places.
verseByVerse.commentary: “The whole armor” (panoplian) — not selected pieces but the full military kit, nothing omitted. It is described as “of God” — divine provision, not human manufacture. Its purpose is to stand (stēnai) — not advance but hold the ground already won in Christ. The enemy is named with military precision: not flesh and blood (the visible human world, however hostile) but rulers, authorities, cosmic powers, spiritual forces of evil in heavenly places. The warfare is spiritual, cosmic, and invisible. Sproul: “The church’s greatest mistakes have come either from denying there is a war, or from fighting the wrong enemy.” (cf. 1 Pet. 5:8–9; 2 Cor. 10:4)

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore take up the whole armour of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The evil day” may be any day of intense spiritual assault, or the eschatological climax of all things. Either way, the goal is to stand — not to advance territory but to hold what has been given. The armour is defensive in orientation, yet absolutely necessary. No piece can be dispensed with.

PREACHER’S NOTE Sproul notes that the image of “having done all, to stand” implies that there will be days when you have done everything right and still face fierce attack. Faithfulness is not immunity from assault; it is readiness for it.

verseByVerse.quote: having fastened on the belt of truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and, as shoes for your feet, having put on the readiness given by the gospel of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary: The first three pieces of armor address the core of personal integrity and standing. The belt of truth — integrity of life, alignment of inner and outer, the opposite of the devil who is the father of lies. The breastplate of righteousness — the imputed righteousness of Christ, guarding the heart against accusation and condemnation; not moral achievement but the alien righteousness received by faith alone. The shoes of the gospel of peace — the Roman soldier’s caligae gave firm footing and readiness to move; the gospel gives believers stability in treacherous spiritual terrain and readiness to carry the good news wherever the battle leads.

verseByVerse.quote: In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God,
verseByVerse.commentary: “In all circumstances” (en pasin) — the shield of faith is not situational but constant. The Roman thureos was a large door-shaped shield soldiers could interlock in formation; faith is a community discipline as much as a personal one. The flaming darts — accusations, temptations, deceits — are extinguished by faith in Christ’s finished work. The helmet of salvation guards the mind from despair and doubt, anchoring it in the certainty of final deliverance. And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God — the only offensive weapon in the list, the rhema of God wielded by the Spirit, cutting through every deception. Jesus used it in the wilderness (Matt 4); it remains the weapon of the church’s advance. (cf. Heb. 4:12; Matt. 4:4)

verseByVerse.quote: praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication. To that end, keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints,
